item.title: He Never Won Elected Office, Yet He Reshaped All of New York
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-stuffmissed-他从未当选任何公职-却重塑了整座纽约/

item.description: Robert Moses stacked appointed positions into power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Moses stacked appointed positions into power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.

This episode has medium information density, but how Moses accumulated power through unelected positions, and the exact words from his 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, are valuable for understanding urban governance and how power operates.

1:01 Never elected, yet he held enormous power
Robert Moses was never elected to any public office in his life, yet he accumulated enormous power through appointment to various government positions. According to Encyclopaedia Britannica, his work included 35 highways, 12 bridges, numerous parks, Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, Shea Stadium, many housing projects, two hydroelectric plants, and the 1964 New York World's Fair. He has been dead 45 years and remains a divisive figure, and his legacy may be argued over for another century or more.

6:10 His mentor taught him not to anger voters
Moses became chief of staff of the New York State Reconstruction Commission in 1919 and learned a great deal from Belle Moskovitz. Moskovitz understood deeply how to maneuver within government to achieve goals without antagonizing those in power. One example: in an early draft of a report, Moses suggested cutting part of the workforce, and Moskovitz reminded him that every one of those people was a voter, that they could not be angered, and that he had to find a way to cut costs without cutting that many people. This ‘don't anger the voters’ thinking ran through his later government work.

11:11 Parks were the means, highways were the end
When Moses took over the parks commission, most green-space plans merely preserved natural wilderness, but he envisioned adding more manicured landscaping and dedicated recreation areas. More importantly, every time he built a new park, he made sure the project included roads connecting the park to highways — that is where the parkway came from. From the start he planned a large state park system for Long Island, all linked by new roads. In just four years in office, he added 13 parks to Long Island, about 9,700 acres in total, where previously there had been only one park.

13:14 His mother lent him $20,000 to save Jones Beach
Jones Beach was originally just a sandbar on the southern edge of Long Island, almost completely submerged at high tide. Moses wanted to turn it into a great park, and most of the government and the press considered it impractical. He first used large-scale dredging to dig about 40 million cubic yards of sand from the seabed, raising the sandbar from two feet above sea level to twelve feet. But the project nearly died when the money ran out, and Moses did something highly unusual: he borrowed $20,000 from his mother Bella to continue the work. He later confirmed that if his mother had not put up the money, the contractor would not have brought the equipment back to finish. Jones Beach finally opened on August 4, 1925, in a dust storm, and an estimated 1.5 million people visited in its first year.

22:31 His only campaign, and he lost badly
Moses ran for public office only once in his life. In 1934 he ran for governor of New York and was thoroughly defeated by the incumbent Democratic governor, Herbert H. Lehman. Lehman received more than 2.2 million popular votes; Moses got fewer than 1.4 million. Reporting Lehman's victory, The New York Times wrote: ‘Meanwhile his formidable and pugnacious opponent, Robert Moses, will be free to continue his work as the great parks commissioner.’ After this defeat he never tried to run for office again, and instead continued to expand his power through appointed positions.

23:33 235 new playgrounds, only one in Harlem
Beginning in the 1930s, Moses greatly expanded the city's playgrounds, building 235 new ones. But a pattern began to emerge: he ignored the needs of districts with predominantly non-white populations. Of the 235 playgrounds, only one was in Harlem. In the summer of 1936 he opened 11 new swimming pools: 4 in Manhattan (including one in Harlem and one in West Harlem), 4 in Brooklyn, and 1 each in the Bronx, Queens, and Staten Island. These pools had new filtration and chlorination systems, heating, and underwater lighting, and were considered advanced, but they were also designed to be drained in the cooler months and used for other activities, from shuffleboard to roller skating.

24:35 ‘Clear the slums, just build a road’
In a 1945 article in The Atlantic Monthly, Moses opened by describing how slums form: existing buildings overcrowded, speculators adding tenants, people packed into tenements like chickens. But the ‘cure’ he offered was this: slum clearance in most cities is accomplished indirectly — not for public, semi-public, or private housing, but for parks, playgrounds, parkways, highways, boulevards, and other public improvements. He boasted that his ‘demolition and construction demon squad’ had torn down more old slums than all the housing experts combined, and that ‘we built nothing but broad highways, flanked by landscaping and recreational facilities.’

33:43 Eminent domain is the only salvation
In the article Moses explicitly endorsed the use of eminent domain to acquire land. He wrote that buying large tracts of land at a reasonable price was no longer possible, and that in such a situation, ‘eminent domain is the only salvation.’ Eminent domain must be exercised by the city, state, or federal government for private limited-dividend or redevelopment companies. He also criticized unions as ‘a serious obstacle to financing slum clearance,’ accusing them of insisting on retaining hourly wage rights, striking, and ‘resisting invention and improvement in the building field.’ He said this attitude was ‘unreasonable’ and would not change until a better-educated new generation of union officials appeared.

item.title: Chinese open-weight models lead, and distillation explains only one to two months of the gap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-interconnects-中国开源权重模型领先-蒸馏只解释一两个月差距/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-interconnects-中国开源权重模型领先-蒸馏只解释一两个月差距/
item.description: Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap — the real reasons are release cadence and task focus; US companies are already building products on Chinese models.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap — the real reasons are release cadence and task focus; US companies are already building products on Chinese models.

This is a state-of-open-models briefing for Congress: dense with data and clear in its judgments, suited to anyone who wants to grasp the US-China open-model landscape quickly.

0:00 Open weights is not the same as open source
An open-weight model releases only the weights and a license; an open-source model also releases the training code and data. America's genuinely open-source models are led by non-profits, such as the Allen Institute for AI's Olmo, OpenAthena's Marin, and EleutherAI's Pythia. Nvidia's Nemotron is more open than most open-weight models, having released a large amount of training data, but because it has not released all of it, it still does not count as fully open source. The distinction matters: when people discuss ‘open source’, what they actually mean is mostly open weights.

0:00 Chinese models have crossed the agentic capability threshold
GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3 delivered a step change in commercial viability, crossing an agentic capability threshold similar to the one Anthropic's Claude Code crossed in December 2025. Chinese open-weight models passed the US in these two key areas roughly 18 months ago. On Hugging Face downloads, China took the lead in July 2025, mainly on the back of Alibaba's Qwen. Data from the ATOM project, which the author maintains, shows China's download lead has grown to about 1.6 billion out of a total of 3.2 billion — twice that of the US.

0:00 The benchmark score gap is stark
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, as of September 14, 2026, the top three are Chinese models: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash score 45 and 42, and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 scores 44. The US leaders are Thinking Machines' Inkling and Inkling Small, both scoring 26, and Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 23. The top US models were released in June and July 2026, and update less frequently than their Chinese counterparts. Chinese labs are closest on tasks with well-defined demand such as agentic coding, and lag further behind on open-ended scientific tasks such as physics and biology.

0:00 Distillation explains only one to two months of the gap
Distillation is a technique Chinese labs use commonly, training their own models on the outputs of stronger models, but the author estimates that even if distillation were blocked entirely — say by deploying KYC tools at Anthropic and OpenAI — the gap from the strongest US models to Chinese open-weight models would widen by only 1-2 months. Distillation matters most in new domains, and it cannot easily produce a comprehensively strong final model. Chinese labs release faster and with a narrower task distribution, which slightly inflates scores on public benchmarks, because all labs keep improving and later-released models naturally score higher.

0:00 US companies are building products on Chinese models
Harvey, Cursor and DoorDash use Kimi, Airbnb uses Qwen, and Perplexity uses DeepSeek. A large number of young Silicon Valley startups use Chinese models to get a low-cost, flexible option. US startups sign enterprise agreements with Chinese model labs to license products for use — a new form of cross-border technology cooperation the author has not seen in his career. On OpenRouter, the Chinese model share has grown from about 70% to more than 80%, and weekly processed tokens have grown from about 1 trillion in September 2025 to about 80 trillion today. On OpenCode, Chinese models account for about 95% or more of inference volume.

0:00 Academia has already been taken over by Qwen
The author scanned papers in the five most popular ML categories on arXiv (cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.LG, stat.ML). In January 2023, papers mentioning any open model were 2%; by September 2026 they reached 50%. In April-May 2023, of about 12,000 new papers, 2,600 mentioned at least one open-model family, 5.5% mentioned Llama, and 1% mentioned Chinese models. At Llama's peak in autumn 2024, 23% mentioned Llama and 7.5% mentioned Qwen. Today Llama is still mentioned by about 21% of papers, while Qwen has risen to 30%. Any Chinese open-weight model is mentioned by more than 40% of papers, versus 30% for the US.

0:00 US models see higher adoption at equal capability
Research shows that US models enjoy disproportionately high adoption when capability and scale are comparable. OpenAI's gpt-oss, its first open-weight models after ChatGPT, became one of the most widely adopted open-weight models ever. Google's Gemma 4 is one of the few models whose adoption approaches Qwen's most popular small models. Nvidia's Nemotron, despite being more capable at the same scale, has seen middling adoption. This shows US models have brand and ecosystem advantages, but not enough to reverse the overall trend.

0:00 Open-model risk requires ecosystem-level preparation
The structural challenge of open-weight models is that there is almost no effective way to stop pieces of open-source software from falling into the wrong hands. If access to China's strongest open-weight models were restricted because of risk, it would be US companies that suffered. HuggingFace once used a Chinese open-weight model to understand a cyberattack, because closed models refused the request. Managing open-weight model risk tends to come down to ecosystem preparation. Open models are becoming an essential tool for AI diffusion, and continuing to invest in US open models is the best path to staying ahead of these risks.

item.title: Poetry Is Not Democracy's Ornament but Its Pillar
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.description: Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free speech just like censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape entirely through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.
item.content:encoded:
Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free speech just like censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape entirely through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.

Not a literature class: a working poet who also heads the largest humanities funder in the country explains why close reading, naming and literacy are political capacities; the second half is harder than the opening.

5:32 The poet went to the scene instead of writing reflections
Rukeyser was not a poet who stayed in the study. At 19, while studying at Vassar, she felt she had to go south to sit in on the Scottsboro trial — staying at school simply wasn't an option; in 1936 she went to Spain to see the counter-Olympiad against the Berlin Games and arrived just as the Spanish Civil War broke out; she also went to West Virginia to write about the Hawks Nest mine disaster — Union Carbide dug tunnels without wet drilling and without giving workers protective gear, the workers were mostly African American, and nearly all died of silicosis, which Alexander says may be the largest corporate industrial accident in American history. The conclusion: writing lets more people know what happened, and connects people of different identities on shared human experience.

13:50 Art is democracy's pillar, not its illustration
She breaks democracy down into a question of language: who a collective is, what it values, which voices it contains — all of it takes shape through language, so without language there is no collective. When we talk about free speech we always stare at journalism, but artists being censored, books being banned, teachers being told what they can teach — that moves the same foundation. Her wording is hard: art is not democracy's explanatory diagram, art is itself part of democracy — one of its pillars. And poetry doesn't just wave a flag for values; it is the thing itself. To judge whether a democracy is healthy, look at whether art can still live in an unconstrained space.

33:37 Close reading is critical thinking, and it can be taught
She describes close reading very plainly: a method, a practice, anyone can learn it, and its other name is critical thinking. Its use isn't limited to poems — you use it reading the newspaper, reading the propaganda around you, whether that propaganda comes from above or from advertising and very, very powerful culture. Figuring out how someone is working on you is a good thing. And in America many people are nervous about poetry, feeling they ‘shouldn't be able to understand it’; her method is concrete: drop your shoulders, read it again, don't just read it on the page, read it aloud, then you read it to me — the same poem read by a different person, and you hear something different every time.

42:37 Misnaming people is an anti-democratic weapon
She says one of the most powerful weapons against democracy is misnaming people, calling people by the wrong name. There's an American saying, calling people out of their names, which means flattening people, using insulting labels, even smearing the behaviour of an entire people as a whole — that's an abuse of language, its purpose is to wound and divide, and it is coming from the highest levels of government. She stresses one thing in particular: it has real consequences. Conversely, naming things precisely, saying what you mean, saying who you are, and catching what others say — that itself is the capacity democracy needs.

47:58 Put grief into language and only then can you hold it
Her husband Fikre died 14 years ago. She wrote a memoir shortly after his death, which surprised even her — she had never imagined writing one or showing it to anyone; it was more a way of landing, of knowing what she was going through: too overwhelming, too unprecedented, and turning some of it into language helped her name the feeling. Writing about him years later was different in kind, became a responsibility: this person was her ‘my person’, who lived a brave, extraordinary, beautiful life and left hundreds of paintings, now shown in museums and galleries. She is wary of herself too: I hope I'm not wringing this experience dry.

57:30 Writing a poem throws away far more than it keeps
She doesn't start a poem from ‘I want to write a poem about X’ but from a word, an image, a phrase that rings there, and she can't say why, so she writes it down again and again. She has a day job — almost all poets do — so the real question is: while you're busy with something else, where do you put the thought. Fragments accumulate slowly, and when there's time to sit down, you ask which piece is still vibrating, still alive. How much do you write versus throw away? Her answer is one word: Most. A serious writer throws away many times what they keep, and that takes a little courage — keep writing even when it's wrong. What really excites her is the editing stage, because ‘the beast is there’, the outline is already visible.

1:02:17 The cost of college is a problem, learning is not
She directly rebuts the claim that the humanities have no prospects: critical thinking, close reading, extracting meaning from complex texts, communicating persuasively, imagining other people's lives, understanding multiple cultures — these are capacities useful in any career. She doesn't deny that the cost of higher education is a real problem that really needs solving, but she puts the emphasis elsewhere: what's more worrying is the attack on the university itself, interference in its mission, and the claim that ‘the university is not a valuable thing’ being repeated loudly. Her last line is sharp: creating an undereducated populace serves another purpose.

1:07:22 Those who cannot read are the easiest to control
‘free people read freely’ is a line from the poet and librarian Tracie D. Hall, and Alexander says she borrows it all day long. She reads those five words from the African American tradition: under slavery, it was a crime for Black people to learn to read and write, and it was equally a crime for a free white person to teach them — what was being controlled was not the text, it was the people. So the line holds two halves: free people read freely, and, free people are meant to read. If a person cannot read, cannot access a mass of information, they cannot understand their own life, and they lose the capacity to act on an understanding of how outside forces work on them. Where literacy is stripped away, there is only one logic: this is how you are easier to control.

item.title: Literacy Once Democratised Europe; Now It Is Going Backwards
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.description: Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are now dragging public discourse back toward the pre-literate age.
item.content:encoded:
Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are now dragging public discourse back toward the pre-literate age.

Medium information density, but two mechanisms are worth hearing: "writing cools discourse" and "bad ideas are easier to whitewash on film"; the later section on pop music and reading is looser.

8:13 Literacy is historically extremely recent and fragile
Marriott stresses that we are so used to literacy that we forget how anomalous it is. By one estimate, in a certain ancient Mesopotamian city-state there may have been only 20 living people who could read and write; literacy in ancient Rome was around 10%. For thousands of years, reading and writing was not a cultural phenomenon but an esoteric code circulating within a wealthy scribal elite — some rulers were literate, some were not. The real turning point was printing: books could be reproduced in quantity, more people could read, and books became more practical; Protestantism then placed enormous emphasis on the written word, pushing more people to become literate in order to read the Bible. These factors fed each other until the "Reading Revolution" historians identify in the mid-to-late 18th century.

11:19 The Reading Revolution really did change the shape of politics
Roberts pushes back: if literacy exploded, why doesn't the world look turned upside down? Marriott's answer is that the spread of literacy has a democratising effect — the more people who can access information and ideas, the more people participate in politics and criticise power. Early 18th-century Europe was ruled by absolute monarchs; political affairs were essentially court secrets, discussed only among a small elite. By the late 18th and early 19th centuries, newspapers appeared, the standing of absolute monarchs declined sharply, France became a republic, the authority of the British monarch was far weaker than at the start of the century, parliamentary debates were reported, and public affairs were no longer discussed only in court. He calls this the great age of democratic revolution and democratic reform, and ties it directly to the spread of literacy.

16:32 Writing forces bad ideas into logical form
Marriott concedes books are imperfect, but argues that the way a book organises information is more rational and more coherent than conversation, video or TikTok. Writing forces you to polish an idea repeatedly, externalising part of your mind onto the page and then testing it; the reader faces a fixed text and can reread and analyse it critically. More crucially, the book limits the means of non-logical persuasion — you cannot bypass argument with charisma, shouting or tears. He uses the Nazis as a counterexample: Hitler's Mein Kampf was unreadable even to the Nazi elite, because Nazism simply does not hold together once it is required to be presented coherently as a written text; yet Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will is treated as an artistic masterpiece, screened in film classes, and regarded as an extremely powerful argument for fascism. Bad ideas are easier to whitewash on screen than in a book.

25:05 The Republic of Letters filtered out the trolls through writing
The 17th- and 18th-century European "Republic of Letters" was a community of thinkers, philosophers and scientists who wrote letters to one another and ran journals. The economic historian Joel Mokyr rates it extraordinarily highly, saying it is the single cultural fact that explains the Industrial Revolution. Marriott's mechanism is this: if a clever person sits alone in a village, his ideas can only be told to his neighbours, and scientific innovation struggles to accumulate; the spread of literacy let ideas travel further, more and more people joined the conversation, ideas flowed into a central pool, and thought grew more complex. Roberts adds that the key difference is not public versus private but who the participants are — in conversation with Adam Smith, David Hume, Newton, the standard is naturally high; it is a kind of "submission to that which cannot be enforced". Marriott concedes that the literacy barrier itself carries a benign elitism: you cannot burst in and shout like a troll on X, because nobody will engage with you.

34:49 The novel gives us a passage into other minds
Marriott argues there is a truth about life that only prose fiction can reach: it lets us see the inside of other people's minds. Reading is an active rather than passive process — you use the words on the page to build images in your head, which is why it is immersive, why it feels like having lived another life. Film cannot do this, because it gives you the external world and cannot enter another mind directly; and writing is precisely the medium we use to express what is in our minds, a communication of mind to mind. He also notes that oral poetry takes little interest in the subtle differences between human consciousnesses, and that this capacity to "inhabit another mind" appears only in prose fiction. Roberts does not fully agree, holding that great film can approach it through dialogue, but concedes that film almost never captures the inner activity that is conveyed by more than dialogue.

47:59 The post-literate commentator is more like Homer
Marriott writes that the post-literate commentator does not explain and analyse the world like the print-age public intellectual, but is more like an oral storyteller, weaving strange and unforgettable tales for a captivated audience. Roberts calls this the deepest insight in the whole piece: faced with the mass of absurd, untenable statements online, people habitually interrogate them by the author's standards — "that isn't logical", "where's the evidence?" — but these people are simply not in that business. Their job is to entertain the audience; truth does not matter, what matters is a story that captivates. Marriott goes further: presenting an argument logically, supplying evidence, pushing through to a rational conclusion — these are not in fact natural to human communication; in an oral culture, the more effective way to persuade someone is to entertain him, move him, get angry at him. Writing imposes an impersonal, more rational form of communication, and it is not a necessary product of human communication.

53:59 The richness of pop music also feeds off reading
Roberts cites an example from The History of Rock and Roll in 500 Songs: Jagger wrote "Sympathy for the Devil", whose opening is taken directly from Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita — that novel opens with two Russian intellectuals mocking God and faith, after which a suave gentleman appears, they think he is mad, and finally they realise it is Satan. Marriott calls this an "annoyingly good" example and regrets not having put it in the book. He concedes it cannot be pushed too far — it is not that you have to move Penguin Classics into the British Library to join a boy band — but Bob Dylan and Paul McCartney are both obviously heavy readers. He cites research showing that over the past 20 years pop songs have become less complex in both lyrics and melody, partly because the environment favours simplicity and immediacy: to go viral on TikTok, a song has to grab you within three or four seconds.

58:17 The future of reading will be deliberate, like fitness
Marriott stresses this is not a new phenomenon: statistics on the decline of serious reading go back to the 1950s and 1960s; television was the beginning of the screen age, and the remote control was the first scroll. Roberts quotes what his father said at the time — books have existed for centuries, television has been a mass medium for only 20 years, let's see if it lasts — and concedes his father should have worried more. Marriott's consolation comes from the analogy with junk food and fitness: McDonald's arrived, many people got fat, but some realised that health could no longer be absorbed naturally from the environment and required deliberate effort, so they started running and going to the gym. He guesses cognitive health will follow the same path: if reading has a future, it will become more deliberate, less "I'm bored at the airport, I'll pick up a book" and more "I value this experience, so I sit down for half an hour to an hour every night". He admits this makes him a little sad, because reading will become more artificial, no longer the unavoidable part of life it once was.

item.title: A Glass of Water Has No Final Truth: Quantum Mechanics Forces Us to Give Up the Single Perspective
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.description: Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not new particles, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is multiple perspectives that enrich one another but do not converge.
item.content:encoded:
Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not new particles, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is multiple perspectives that enrich one another but do not converge.

A four-person roundtable crossing physics, poetry, drama and economics; high density of quotable lines but the argument is loose. Worth listening if you want a few perspectives that can change your judgment; skip it if you want hard information.

2:06 A glass of water has no final version
Rovelli opens with a glass of water the BBC provided: you look from one side, I look from the other, you wear glasses, I see a different colour. This glass of water can be a physical object (mass, velocity, position), it can be temperature and pressure, it can be the chemistry of H2O plus floating bits, it can be the global economy of being bottled in Italy and shipped to England, or it can simply be ‘we want to drink it’. His claim is that all these perspectives are real, none exhausts another, none contradicts another, and there is no ‘ultimate glass of water’. This is anti-Platonic — he does not accept a distinction between a ‘level of appearances’ and a ‘fundamental level’.

6:13 We have not yet digested quantum mechanics
Rovelli says what he is describing is not borrowed from philosophy but grown from inside physics. Physicists ran into quantum phenomena; quantum mechanics is a huge revolution, but ‘we have not yet digested quantum mechanics’ — the newspaper stories about experiments that ‘confirm what I learned in a textbook in the 1970s’ show precisely that we do not yet truly believe it. Take quantum mechanics seriously and what it says is this: the Enlightenment dream of ‘a complete, determinate, clear description of reality independent of the observer’ does not hold. The observer here need not be a human; anything that interacts with something else counts.

8:19 The most fundamental reality is not more objective
Rovelli turns it around: the reality at the most basic level physics can reach is in fact not essentially different from the reality Lavinia deals with in poetry, or the characters in James's play deal with in economics — both are realities that allow different views, not a reality that is ‘absolutely objective underneath’. So quantum physics is not that hard; it has simply not been digested. The concrete physical phenomena are of course very complex, but poetry is complex and economics is complex too.

10:25 Scientists have always used metaphors
Rovelli says the words Lavinia uses could be lifted line by line into his book. What is an electron? ‘It is a grain, a grain of sand, but it is not really a grain of sand.’ Why is an electric field called a field? Because it is ‘a bit like a field in the countryside’. We think through metaphor, by taking old concepts apart and piecing together a new concept from a bit of each. The goal is not to arrive at a final perfect description of reality — a century ago we thought we could, but it does not work — but to gain better understanding, better ways of navigating reality. He adds a crucial qualification: admitting that everything has a perspective does not mean all perspectives are equivalent, nor that there is no better and worse; it is only that the hope of ‘arriving at the final correct story about reality’ is empty — not unreachable, but meaningless.

12:27 Seeking the ultimate morality is itself wrong
Rovelli turns from ‘complexity’ to ‘value’: if you ask ‘what is the ultimate definition of good and evil, what is universal ethics’, he thinks this is itself a morally and ethically wrong approach. Our morals and values are powerful, important and indispensable not because they are outside us, but because they are inside us, and therefore equally perspectival. This passage connects directly to James Graham's play — whose first line is ‘what is a good life’.

15:30 Do not be afraid to learn a jargon
Lavinia Greenlaw argues for embracing jargon: not everyone has to learn it, but if you are genuinely interested in something, do not be afraid to learn its language — a mechanic has to learn the names of parts, a surgeon has to learn the names of parts, a poet has to learn too. It lets you see more clearly, and it lets you see where something has gone wrong. She admits jargon can be exclusionary, but ‘that depends on the context in which you use it’, and ‘you can perform difficulty, poets and poems are probably very good at that, but that is not what difficulty means’. She gives the example of poems on the Underground: before everyone looked at their phones, people would read a poem first and only then realise they were reading a poem — that kind of engagement is far more direct and confident than sitting down and being told ‘now you are going to read a poem’.

22:55 Friction is treated as a problem to be solved
James Graham says modern culture fetishises ‘efficiency’ and strips out every layer of difficulty as friction. He gives a concrete image: emailing himself a script to save it, and a prompt pops up, ‘This is a long document, shall I summarise it for you?’ — his reaction was ‘how rude, I want you to sit inside it and read’. He connects back to Bloomsbury and Keynes: meaning is discovered precisely in the friction, in the difficulty, in the process. He also says the collapse of reading is despairing, because reading demands personal investment, and today that investment is treated as a problem to be solved rather than something to be celebrated.

26:05 War refuses to acknowledge complexity
Rovelli uses International Peace Day on 21 September, and remarks by the UN Secretary-General and the Pope, to connect the perspectival argument to war: war is to a large extent driven by greed and power games, but it always wraps itself in a hypocritical narrative — there is only one truth, only one good, we are the good ones, they are the bad ones, we tell the truth, they tell lies and propaganda. So war is built on a total refusal to be prepared to accept complexity, perspectives, and worldviews different from our own. The host Adam Rutherford raises a counterexample on the spot: we also always need to seek simplicity; if we embraced difficulty and acted scholarly all day, we might get nothing done and enjoy nothing. Lavinia's response pulls the topic back to rhetoric: language therefore matters more than ever, and poetry and poetics can teach people to argue.

item.title: Apple has no frontier model of its own, but wants to win again with a foldable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.description: Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event had not one new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on the foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.
item.content:encoded:
Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event had not one new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on the foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.

Mark Gurman is the most accurate reporter on Apple, and this episode threads executive turnover, the AI roadmap, the privacy controversy and foldable predictions into one line, with high information density.

5:09 The biggest difference between Ternus and Cook is willingness to make the call
Gurman says the event was almost interchangeable with the Cook era, with the only difference being that Ternus opened by offering a view on AI. The mechanism he gives is management style: you bring an idea to Cook and he keeps probing with questions, in many cases not making a single decision — it's collective decision-making; you bring it to Ternus and he gives you a decision, gives you an opinion, you may hate the opinion, but he has a position. Gurman stresses this is exactly the biggest difference between the two men from talking to insiders, and it explains why Ternus talked about AI first thing on stage.

8:20 The 2026 event had not one new AI feature
Gurman points out that Apple held a big product event in September 2026 and launched no notable new AI features; the opening 15 minutes or so just retold the Apple Intelligence story of the past two years. His explanation: Apple has gone as far on AI as it can and can only tell the best story with the cards it holds; and Apple has no AI-centric device, so it has to prop up the iPhone as its AI device until a killer device appears and it can switch narratives.

13:29 Under Cook, Apple became an institution
Gurman distinguishes the Cook era from the Jobs era: in the Cook era people's relationship with Apple is a relationship with an institution — global, enormous, like IBM; the Jobs era was one category-redefining new product after another. He also corrects the host's read on Vision Pro — every time he writes that Vision Pro is on life support, he gets dozens of responses at the level of near death threats, because some people have built businesses around spatial computing and some consumers paid four thousand dollars for it.

20:45 Apple spent five years swapping out the old guard one by one
Gurman reconstructs the rhythm of the handover: in 2023 Cook began saying at every executive meeting that succession had to be taken seriously; at the time the top ranks either had five hundred million on the books or were billionaires, and were close in age. So they lined up an order and went one by one — at the end of 2024 CFO Luca Maestri retired, replaced by Kevin Parekh; in 2025 COO Jeff Williams retired, succeeded by his deputy; in 2026 the general counsel changed, with Jennifer Newstead poached from Meta; and only at the end of 2026 did Cook hand the baton to Ternus. Gurman calls this retention strategy Hotel California: you never want to leave.

28:07 The chip chief was kept with a title invented on the spot
Gurman says the second most important person at Apple now is the hardware head, who built Apple Silicon, Apple's key differentiator. In late summer or early autumn last year he went to tell Cook he was quitting, right in the middle of preparations for Ternus to take over. Cook got him to stay through the transition and promised him the title of chief hardware officer, which Apple had never had, letting him keep his existing team and also take over Ternus's side of the business. Gurman judges this is not a long-term arrangement and that the man already wants to leave again — he conquered the Mac, shed Intel and Qualcomm, and Apple has no next target, so he may leave within a year or two, at which point the hardware engineering team will have to be split up again, because no successor carries his industry weight.

33:15 Willing to spend tens of billions on a modem, yet says it needn't own AI
What Gurman finds most absurd is executives saying in interviews over the past year that "we never owned search, we don't need to own AI." He counters: these are two completely different things, and Apple spent tens of billions to own an already commoditized cellular modem, acquiring and fixing Intel's modem business — willing to do that for a modem but unwilling to own AI is ridiculous. The internal idea was originally to partner with Google as a stopgap until it could build its own models, but Gurman says he has seen no evidence that Apple is restarting its own model effort, making big AI acquisitions, or paying AI researchers top dollar.

48:53 The watch's always-on transcription stepped on the privacy landmine
Gurman's reaction to the Apple Watch's always-on listening feature was "I can't believe they did it." The feature only transcribes, doesn't record or store, and a double tap shows you the last 15 seconds of what someone said to you, without their consent. He says Apple knows the next-generation interface needs some degree of ambient capture, but the societal privacy problem is unsolved: technical white papers, private cloud compute and encryption can't hold back the social backlash. He thinks Apple could have put audio and visual intelligence together next year and told one coherent privacy story; as it is, it's boiling the frog.

57:05 Foldables will become the new normal within a decade
Gurman offers a bold prediction: foldables will become the new normal within a decade. He draws an analogy with smartphone penetration — at the end of 2006 smartphones were about 6% of the market, now they're 85%, and within five or six years they were past half; the iPhone itself wasn't that source, but it pulled everyone into the smartphone game, and he thinks the iPhone Duo will do the same for the phone market. He also mentions the iPhone's number migration feature, hinting at a future combination of a foldable for work and a smaller, lighter phone for weekends with family.

item.title: America's Manufacturing Hollow-Out Isn't a Capability Problem, It's a Financial-Return Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.description: Chris Power says the US manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement while China manages it like national security; tariffs are only an imperfect corrective tool — the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing a rival's industrial capacity.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Power says the US manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement while China manages it like national security; tariffs are only an imperfect corrective tool — the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing a rival's industrial capacity.

Two frontline hardware founders lay out the real bottlenecks of American reindustrialization: not technology, but trust, cost, and how you define a supply chain. High information density; the back half on tariffs and subsidies is the most valuable part.

2:02 The reserve currency is the first step of decline
Chris Power gives a four-step cycle: a great power first has a generative population and the best industrial capacity, then wins or prevents a war, then becomes extremely lazy, and finally outsources the very things that made it successful. He says this cycle repeats roughly every 150 years — the Dutch gave way to the British, the British gave way to the Americans, and each time industrial power was re-traded for financial power, the world's reserve currency changed hands. That judgment was the starting point for his founding Hadrian: you think you're Mike Tyson at his peak, and your opponent thinks you're the Mike Tyson right before Buster Douglas knocked him out.

9:10 90% of the factory floor is a software problem
Chris Power says the biggest misconception about advanced manufacturing is that when people see someone moving things in a factory, they assume it's a humanoid robot problem. In reality, 90% of advanced manufacturing is smart people sitting at computers doing digital engineering, or operating an extremely dumb computer on the shop floor. A welder or machinist has to stand in front of the machine because the system isn't closed-loop — they're doing trigonometry in their head, judging whether the tool is about to snap. That's why Hadrian positions itself as a software company: its job is to break physical tasks into high-judgment setups, then hand execution to robots, CNCs, or welding systems.

14:14 Software is built in Silicon Valley, hardware in Los Angeles
Tom Mueller says Southern California's aerospace talent ecosystem is recovering — three or four years after SpaceX was founded in 2002, the aerospace employment curve in the South Bay started turning up. He lists what this area is doing simultaneously: nuclear companies, drone companies, defense companies, 3D printing companies, plus Anduril in Orange County. The two companies poach from each other and compete for the same talent; Northrop Grumman is right across the street from Impulse. Tom's summary: software is built in Silicon Valley, hardware is built in Los Angeles.

15:17 Vertical integration is for learning the problem, not saving money
Tom Mueller explains the real logic of SpaceX-style vertical integration: you have to build the first development engine or spacecraft yourself, because in the prototype phase you need to learn every assembly and machining problem. If you hand it to a machine shop from the start, and the drawing is wrong and the part doesn't fit when it comes back, you learn nothing. Once the design converges, you outsource. Chris Power adds that every company should keep 10% to 15% of its capacity in-house, because there's always a "hot pot" moment when you need a genius to make something within an hour to hit a flight milestone — but scale has to happen outside.

16:18 Outsourcing decisions run on trust, not finance
Chris Power says what's bought and sold in manufacturing is trust. Hadrian's vertical integration strategy is to outsource as much as possible to every reindustrialization startup and small business, because there are too many projects to run. But they vertically integrate the links where they "don't believe you can deliver on time" — that's not a financial trade-off, it's a willingness to spend an extra two million dollars on equipment and hire a team rather than bet the risk on a legacy foundry that has been late on every submarine program for the past thirty years. His exact words: most of America is incompetent at trust and scheduling.

19:20 In World War II, America was China
Chris Power uses World War II as an analogy: German engineers crushed America on engineering, but America ground them down with McDonald's-style mass production and better logistics. He says America played the role in World War II that China plays today — not by engineering best, but by producing most. Now the situation is reversed: US missile stockpiles run out in seven days in war games, and China built 2,600 ships while America built six. His conclusion: you can have the best Raytheon missile, but if you can't mass-produce it, you have no options.

21:23 The robot bottleneck is the velocity of training data
Chris Power says the robotics race ultimately comes down to software, and software — especially AI — now comes down to the velocity of training data, which in turn depends on physical-world deployment, meaning mass manufacturing. So this isn't a friendly competition between American companies over "whether Tesla sells a few more Optimuses or Google wins" — it's a civilizational-level confrontation. Tom Mueller adds from the space angle: building on the Moon and Mars requires robot legions rather than humans, because the environment is too dangerous and too expensive; a good robot needs three things — dexterous hands, vision, which is basically solved, and an AI brain.

29:40 Tariffs are an imperfect corrective tool
Chris Power says manufacturing has four inputs: energy, labor, cost of capital, and export tariffs. He has run the numbers: even if you set Hadrian's labor cost and energy cost to zero, components imported from China are still three times cheaper than buying raw materials in America and making them yourself. He argues China has run industrial policy as national security since 1985, subsidizing energy, labor, capital, and export tariffs, while America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial-statement return. The problem with tariffs is enforcement: ban China but not Singapore, and Chinese companies route through Singapore; differences in the definition of raw materials versus assembly also end up hurting American firms that import components from Mexico.

item.title: He Cooked the Chickpea Pasta Into Mush, Then Survived by Telling People to Steep It Like Tea
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.description: Banza's first scaled-up production run failed completely: 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said ‘steep it like tea’ and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.
item.content:encoded:
Banza's first scaled-up production run failed completely: 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said ‘steep it like tea’ and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.

The founder's account is unusually dense with failure detail: three scrapped production batches, a kidney stone, being thrown out of the factory, a 30% week-over-week decline. Worth hearing for anyone who wants to know how you survive a near-death moment.

5:14 The starting point wasn't a business insight, it was a stuffy nose
In college Brian's fridge held nothing but hummus, eating was just ‘fuel’ to him, and he cycled between antibiotics and steroids for so long he was nearly facing surgery. It was his father, an orthodontist, who got him to try an elimination diet, and that's how he found that wheat-based foods triggered sinus inflammation — one beer and the next day he couldn't breathe. The ENT told him: I don't know what you're talking about, but if it works, keep doing it. That private problem became the product definition: high-protein, high-fiber, gluten-free pasta, doing what Chobani did for yogurt.

10:26 The first recipe had chia in it and was too sticky to look at
He bought Bob's Red Mill chickpea flour on Amazon and followed blogs for combinations. Version one was chickpeas plus eggs plus chia — the chia made it so sticky the result was ugly. With no rolling pin he used a wine bottle; with no pasta cutter he used a knife, dusting flour on the table as he cut to keep it from sticking. Version two dropped the chia, leaving just chickpeas and eggs, and was clearly better, but to make it usable for more people he added back tapioca starch and xanthan gum and committed to a vegan route. His first capital expenditure was an Atlas Mercado hand-crank pasta machine, about $30 on Amazon. He got up at 5 a.m. every day to make pasta, put on country music, and his roommates thought he was insane.

20:49 Going from 200 pounds an hour to 1,000 magnified every mistake
They first found a tiny gluten-free factory in Michigan that could only do 150 to 200 pounds an hour — wildly inefficient, but they could learn as they went. To get into 190 Meijer stores and 2 Eataly locations, that capacity wasn't enough, so they found what was then the largest gluten-free pasta plant in the country, outside Los Angeles. The problem: that plant had only ever run rice and corn pasta, never legumes. Scaled up to roughly 1,000 pounds an hour, the pasta looked fine coming out and turned into total mush the moment it was boiled. Each trial run was 8,000 to 10,000 pounds, and a failure meant the die costs and ingredient costs were all gone — and they had only a little over $100,000 to their name.

26:02 He got thrown out of the factory for asking the operator
After several failed trial runs, Brian ignored the other side's objections and went straight to the line operator to ask what was actually going wrong. The worker said ‘this corn smells weird,’ and he answered: that's not corn, we're not making corn pasta today, it's chickpeas. He realized on the spot that communication had broken down completely, and right after that he was escorted out of the plant. At the same time the distributor was threatening him: if you don't fulfill this purchase order, you will never work with this retailer again. He later estimated this shipment would cost nearly every dollar they had.

28:07 The fix was don't boil it — steep it like tea
With nowhere left to turn they started testing: boil one minute, two minutes, three minutes, then stop boiling altogether — bring water to a boil, turn off the heat, and let the pasta sit in the hot water. What came out of steeping was better than what came out of boiling, or at least it didn't fall apart. Brian says he wasn't proud of the product, and it bothered him to sell it under his own brand, but he knew it was life or death. The packaging was already printed, so they could only add a sticker reading ‘Banza is easier to cook than regular pasta — steep it like tea,’ and then had people hand-apply it to 20,000 boxes. Once that shipment went out, they immediately pulled out of the big plant and went back to the small one in Michigan.

35:18 The box is orange because every pasta box was blue
They noticed that nearly every pasta package on the shelf at the time was blue — Brian put it as ‘you'd think they'd colluded.’ Orange contrasts most strongly with blue, and orange was also the color he'd loved since watching Nickelodeon as a kid, so it became the brand color. The packaging copy involved trade-offs too: putting ‘chickpeas’ front and center would scare off a lot of people, and so would gluten-free, so the gluten-free certification went on the side while the front led with high protein and high fiber — making consumers feel this was ‘a product for me’ rather than ‘not a product for me.’

41:31 The glyphosate report cut weekly sales by a third
Moms Across America published a report claiming glyphosate residue had been detected in Banza products. Brian saw the Google alert during a one-on-one meeting; he says his heart sank and his mind jumped twenty steps ahead. He wanted to verify first, so he issued only a ‘we are investigating’ statement — which was nowhere near enough for the most panicked people. The lab results were delayed again and again, dragging on for three weeks. The final published result was 98% below the allegation, but not zero — still a very low level, and below the EWG's risk benchmark. He decided to make the supply chain 100% traceable and joined the Detox Project's certification program.

52:15 Natural channel recovered far more slowly than conventional
The sales recovery was a mixed bag: some channels came back better than before, but the natural channel recovered much more slowly — and that was exactly the customer base with the best repeat purchase rates and the highest sales per store. Brian says this actually makes sense, because natural channel consumers are the most susceptible to this kind of information. What he does now: he keeps alerts on for anywhere Banza and glyphosate are mentioned, and personally goes onto Reddit to reply and add context, with the goal of making it impossible for the story to be seen without its context. He also admits he should have acknowledged what was happening faster and more visibly.

item.title: AI won't replace people — what replaces people is work that was never written down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.description: Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of how work gets done — that "map of work" is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own model.
item.content:encoded:
Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of how work gets done — that "map of work" is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own model.

Daniel Dines breaks down the real bottleneck of AI inside the enterprise from UiPath's front-line view, with a high density of counter-consensus claims — suited to anyone trying to judge the pace of enterprise AI adoption.

6:17 AI does not change its own weights on the job
Daniel argues the biggest difference between AI and humans is not reasoning ability, but that AI does not change its own weights on the job. A human is changed by a job; AI just writes things into a notebook. He gives the example of two chefs: one who has cooked Japanese cuisine for 20 years, one who has cooked Italian for 20 years. Give them the same recipe and what they produce is completely different. This is not something you can replicate by writing the company down on paper, because human judgment comes from years of being reshaped by the work. So on the claim that "there are millions of Einsteins in the data center," Daniel thinks what Dario meant is that there are millions of entities with partial reasoning ability — not Einsteins who can learn on the job the way a person does.

16:29 Probabilistic tech shouldn't do work that demands precision
Daniel raises another limit on AI: precision. Every step AI takes is probabilistic, and even if each step is 99% correct, after 100 steps the overall success rate may be down to 60%. So if you have AI do long multiplication over and over, it will eventually get it wrong. His conclusion: just because a tool can do something doesn't mean you should use it for that thing. ChatGPT looks like it is doing arithmetic, but behind the scenes it is calling a computer tool — the precision is not coming from ChatGPT. Extend that logic to the enterprise: all work that demands precision should run on precise technology; there is no reason for it to run on probabilistic technology.

18:34 Deploying AI hasn't gotten easier; deploying automation has
Daniel points to an asymmetry inside the enterprise: deploying AI agents is no easier than it was two years ago, but deploying automation has become much easier, because you can use coding agents to generate the automation. He lists ChatGPT, chain of thoughts and coding agents as the three main milestones. Coding agents work at "design time": people use them to build automation that runs precisely every time at "execution time"; and when automation breaks because an upstream system changed, AI can come back and fix it. The result is that AI is generating the software that runs the company, and that software cannot change its behavior in real time — it can be audited, tested and read by people. This is the pattern he sees taking shape in the enterprise right now.

23:46 Blind layoffs cut the people AI most needs
In his book Daniel introduces the concept of the "credentialed middle": companies used to hire for deep domain credentials in some field, and that is exactly the kind of expertise AI helps with most. His judgment is counterintuitive — you will be inclined to cut the people who are not the biggest experts in the domain, but those are precisely the people you will need to supplement expert work with AI. He gives the example of a law firm: it used to hire 25 interns a year, this year it hired only 4. He agrees most roles will need fewer people, but the key question is "which people." His criterion: keep the people with the most initiative, who can maintain client relationships, who can mentor newcomers, who carry the company culture — because AI cannot show initiative in the human sense.

25:51 What decides whether AI can take over is how clear the framework is
Harry thinks work like finance and accounting is highly verifiable, and therefore easy for AI to replace. Daniel disagrees outright: it is not a question of verifiability, but of whether the work is framed by a framework someone else has already defined. He says finance is precisely an area where the framework is unclear — receive an invoice or an order and there can be different ways to handle it, such as whether Nvidia would ship to OpenAI first, and that rule may never have been written down at all. If the rule is not captured by a framework, AI cannot learn it. So a company must first hand AI the "map of work": all workflows, all exceptions, all processes, all systems. This is also what he keeps stressing: models are interchangeable; the map of work and the processes around it are where the real value lies.

29:01 Interview employees with agents and draw the work as a map
UiPath has launched a technology called cartography, as a discipline that helps companies surface how work actually gets done. Concretely, it uses a product called a cartographer agent to interview real business experts and have them record what they are doing, while the agent follows up in real time: why did you change how you handled this invoice because the zip code was different? Why did you choose another path? That is how exceptions get dug out one by one. Then it aggregates data from multiple people to generate a real-time process map. With that "map of work" in hand, you then use coding agents to design how the process should be transformed, and ultimately, through "printing software," move the process from purely manual point A toward a state where fewer people operate the system and more automation and agentic AI operate it.

34:15 Vibe coding is easy for prototypes, hard for production
Daniel admits UiPath tried vibe coding; at first it looked astonishing, but pushing it into production hit a wall: connectors, permissions, auditing, security — all of it has to be maintained. He gives his own example of writing a procurement tool: initially it was written entirely by AI, but the database schema was completely wrong and someone had to rebuild the structure. His conclusion is that going from prototype to production is where the real work is; writing the code itself is not. In the end you will very likely pay as much as, or more than, the tool you replaced — while also consuming the bandwidth of your best people. So he does not think systems of record like Salesforce will be replaced by vibe coding.

45:34 The opportunity in legal AI is in process, not model calls
Harry does the math: the US legal industry is a $300 billion market, and if 30% of the labor can be replaced, that is $90 billion in revenue. Daniel counters that the $90 billion will not convert into token revenue — maybe only 10%, so a $10 billion token opportunity. His judgment: for legal opinions, open-source models and frontier models are both good enough; what is actually valuable is the custom workflow built around the legal process. If Harvey and Lagora just call a model once for you to get a legal opinion, that is not a hundred-billion-dollar market; but if they really draw the work as a map, build the workflows, and create a legal department for you, the value is far greater.

item.title: Even Legal-Cannabis States Can't Escape: A Federal Ban Is About to Empty the THC Shelves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.description: A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry, and now Congress wants to close it — even states where cannabis is legal will feel it when they lose the cheap alternative.
item.content:encoded:
A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry, and now Congress wants to close it — even states where cannabis is legal will feel it when they lose the cheap alternative.

Eight minutes on how a regulatory loophole grew into an industry and how it gets cut off in one stroke — for anyone watching policy risk and regulatory arbitrage.

0:00 Legal-cannabis states can't escape a federal ban either
Recreational cannabis is legal in half of US states, but the reason THC drinks, vapes and gummies can be sold openly in states that ban cannabis is a loophole left by the 2018 farm bill: it allows low-concentration THC from hemp. After lab processing, that low concentration is enough to mimic a cannabis high, which is how you get Delta 8, Delta 9 — and, as the show jokes, by now Delta 11. Congress now wants to close the loophole, and with a stricter ban. The key is that it's a federal ban, so even if your state has legal cannabis, you get hit.

1:00 What's being banned is a $28 billion industry
The show puts the size at $28 billion and says the industry could disappear before the end of this year. Tennessee has already gone first: since July it has banned most THC hemp products, and a local reporter describes herself as already living in a ‘post-hemp world’. State lawmakers even beat Congress to it, banning full-spectrum CBD and smokable flower first. For retailers, farmers and processors, this isn't a policy debate — it's a choice that has to be made before year-end.

3:07 Farmers are going back from hemp to blackberries and corn
Tennessee farmer Lee Crabtree's farm used to grow mostly CBD-variety hemp, and the new state law makes selling those products illegal, so he's gone back to traditional seasonal crops like blackberries and corn. The family still has the industrial kitchen from its CBD food days, and now his wife Stacy uses that big stainless-steel counter to cut grapes for chicken salad and sell it at the roadside farmers market. Lee says income is down, and if the traditional crops don't sell, he'll have to go find a job. This is what the ban looks like landing on one household.

5:08 The regulator's case: consumers don't know what they're drinking
Tennessee Republican Representative William Lamberth uses a drinks analogy: someone buying a Sprite expects a Sprite, not a beer; someone buying a beer expects a beer, not a tequila; someone buying a tequila expects not to get a Sprite. He says the goal is for consumers to know exactly what they're buying. But even farmers who agree with the logic worry the law goes too far. The show gives the other side too: big companies are laying people off, and some are simply moving states — Emily Schaeferich's company Burning Acre moved from Columbia, Tennessee to North Carolina to keep growing, and she admits ripping up the entire retail, manufacturing and wholesale supply chain ‘definitely costs a lot of money’.

6:10 Moving to another state may be wasted effort
Hemp economist Beau Whitney calls the nationwide ban taking effect in December an ‘extinction-level event’. His mechanism: cannabis can only be grown in certain states, while hemp can be grown and shipped anywhere, so hemp businesses can build supersized capacity, push costs down and ship nationwide; cannabis, by contrast, needs a separate supply chain per state and can't get hemp's economies of scale. The result is that hemp-derived food is far cheaper than the cannabis equivalent. So even in states where recreational cannabis is legal, consumers will feel the squeeze when they lose the cheap alternative.

7:13 The ban also takes out state tax revenue
The show pulls out economies of scale on its own to explain: the more of the same good you produce, the lower the unit cost, and the savings can be passed on to consumers. That also explains why hemp-derived food is cheaper than cannabis products. But consumers aren't the only ones affected. For a lot of state budgets, losing the hemp industry means losing a sizable source of tax revenue — in Tennessee alone, a $54 million budget hole. Beau Whitney also says it could put hundreds of thousands of jobs at risk.

7:13 The delay just moves it from November to December
The White House has urged Congress to postpone or amend the ban, the Senate currently supports it, and the House voted earlier this month to delay it too. But those moves only push the effective date from November to December — a one-month delay. For companies that have already moved states and rebuilt supply chains, a month changes nothing: they may have just moved the whole business only to find the industry destroyed in December.

8:14 Those staying behind switch to fiber hemp
Tennessee farmer Bill Corbin, in Springfield, is preparing the first fiber hemp crop for the French company Hemp-It — the kind used for rope, packaging and auto parts. He says there isn't a person in the industry who didn't know this day was coming, that he thinks the industry was unsustainable to begin with, and he agrees with lawmakers' effort to suppress recreational use of hemp-derived products. But he worries about medical consumers: he's older and has arthritis, relies heavily on full-spectrum CBD, and the products left after the ban may not be strong enough for older people or those trying to avoid opioid painkillers.

item.title: The Bat Doesn't Know What It's Like to Be a Bat Either
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.description: The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.
item.content:encoded:
The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.

The second half of episode 400, and listenable on its own. The first half is about theories of consciousness; the second half unexpectedly slides into animal ethics, and the four of them never do settle their disagreement.

1:07 A bat having an inner world is not the same as being conscious
Christopher summarises Dennett's response: he flatly denies Nagel — we can talk about what it's like to be a bat in all sorts of ways (starting by ruling out the things bats don't do), and with enough information we eventually get there, because "what it's like to be a bat" just is the discriminative, dispositional states the bat has. Dylan supplies the step Dennett actually rejects: drawing on von Uexküll's Umwelt and Innenwelt (surrounding world and inner world), Dennett grants that the bat has an inner world, which isn't crazy; what he won't accept is going straight from "has an inner world" to "therefore consciousness exists," and that latter step is exactly the one Nagel uses to prove consciousness exists. Our mode of access is heterophenomenology: treat the bat's behaviour and physiology as a text in need of interpretation.

5:37 Consciousness is not an all-or-nothing property
Christopher reads out a passage from Dennett: are language-less animals not conscious at all? Dennett says the question shouldn't be taken as a matter of course, because it presupposes "something we've had a great deal of trouble getting away from" — that consciousness is an all-or-nothing property, splitting the universe into two utterly different categories: things that have it and things that don't. That dichotomy is what Dennett wants to dismantle; what he wants is consciousness in degrees. Christopher then offers his own version: he doesn't want to accept property dualism, he wants to deny the hard problem, because subjectivity can perfectly well have a biological and evolutionary explanation — agency and subjectivity co-evolved; a physical process organised from the inside "feeling like something" is a real biological phenomenon.

12:57 The bat doesn't know what it's like to be a bat either
Seth pushes the argument to its extreme: it isn't "we don't know what it's like to be a bat," it's that there is no "what it's like to be a bat as seen from the bat's side" at all; the bat itself doesn't know either, because it lacks the machinery to string experiences into a narrative and give them names. Dylan immediately marks out the cost of that inference: if anything with dynamic activity has its own experience, then atoms count too, and that's panpsychism. Christopher says you don't have to go as far as atoms, but concedes the direction really does sound like panpsychism — he'd rather use a threshold: you need a feedback loop of sensing and acting before you can talk about a new way of being.

14:35 Even plants have a perspective in some sense
Mark digs up a line from Dennett's book: the perspective of a conscious observer is a refined descendant of the primitive perspective of the first replicators, which "divided the world into good and bad" — on that account even plants have a perspective in this sense, and "perspective" becomes a metaphor. Christopher then offers gradualism: from sponges to mantis shrimp to humans, subjectivity accumulates layer by layer, getting thicker and thicker, with a fuzzy threshold in between. Dylan wants to nail the threshold down harder: you can't use "complex" as the criterion, since weather is a complex self-maintaining system too; the difference is that living things can replicate themselves and have a wholeness, so the only thing the Earth lacks is its own replication.

19:47 You are a bunch of things, not a soul
Mark finds Dennett's 1994 reply collection Get Real, which uses snakes as an example: a snake has no central representation of "mouse," it just responds to prey through three separate sensory systems. Dennett's point is that the perceptual system we take to be a single whole is really a crowd of little homunculi each making its own discriminations; you are not an Aristotelian form, a soul, an organisation that runs you — we are all a bunch of things. Christopher objects: failure to integrate information processing doesn't mean there's no self — the two hemispheres of a split-brain patient are also separate, and we don't conclude from that that he has no self; the snake may still have a more ancient, minimal sense of boundary and evaluative experience.

27:39 Reducing experience to discrimination looks a lot like behaviourism
Christopher says he agrees with Dennett 99%, and is stuck on the 1%: when Dennett wants to reduce a person to dispositional states, saying that experiencing red is nothing over and above being able to discriminate red from non-red and being in that discriminative state, it sounds like behaviourism. Seth offers a defence: even if the substrate is just discriminative states, subjective experience, the self, is a composite stitched together out of memory, imagination, representation and symbolic language — it weaves scattered discriminative states into a story with descriptions, meanings and colour, and that story is me. Christopher agrees about the narrative self, but points out that the bat has no metacognitive capacity to construct such a self.

38:54 You can club an iguana, but not a rabbit
Mark says "everyone is a world" is a good moral fiction, but he doesn't know how to apply it to animals: Florida has too many iguanas, and encouraging people to go out and club them he says is completely fine, very humane; swap in a rabbit and he won't accept it. Seth offers an evolutionary explanation: our feelings about animals domesticated over tens of thousands of years, wild animals and reptiles were never the same to begin with, and this doesn't conflict with "the self is a narrative centre of gravity." Christopher anchors it in valence: animals are not reflex machines, they are situated perspectives that evaluate, and that is the reason they enter moral consideration — he says that after reading Lars Chittka's The Mind of a Bee, the way he deals with bees changed.

46:10 Take away caring and nothing of the pain is left
Mark turns to where Dennett discusses pain specifically: what are the functional relations of pain? If you take away "caring about it, wanting to get away from it," take away everything else, and leave only the sensation of pain, then nothing is left — your not liking the pain is itself part of the pain. Mark says this is exactly Dennett's attitude to the philosophical zombie: imagine someone whose biology, reactions and even internal relations are exactly like yours, but the light of consciousness never came on — Dennett thinks this is so absurd that it's hard even to explain to scientists.

item.title: Germany's CDU Falls Out of a State Parliament: The Era of the Centre Is Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.description: The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right command an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.
item.content:encoded:
The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right command an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.

This is a piece of German domestic political commentary, not an interview. Information density is moderate, but it lays out the judgment that "populism has become the mainstream" very clearly — suited to anyone watching where European politics is heading.

0:00 The CDU is shut out of a state parliament for the first time
In the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state election, the CDU won under 5% of the vote and therefore holds no seats in that state parliament — the first time this has happened in the history of the Federal Republic. In the same election the AfD took around 38% of the vote, once again becoming the state's largest party. The author calls this the "final nail in the coffin" for Merz: he may hang on as chancellor for a few more weeks or months, but his authority is gone, his capacity to shape the country fully exhausted — in political language, "a dead man walking."

0:00 The CDU's decline came later than the SPD's but is just as fatal
The CDU is the most important party in postwar German history, governing the Federal Republic for 53 of the past 77 years, and from Adenauer to Kohl to Merkel it left its mark on every aspect of the country. The author points out that in the early 2000s everyone was talking about "the crisis of social democracy," as the SPD fell from over 40% support to record lows; in hindsight, the fate of the centre-left big party was only a leading indicator of a broader crisis of the entire political centre, and the CDU subsequently walked the same road. The era of what Germans call the Volksparteien — catch-all parties capable of mobilising most of the vote — is effectively over.

0:00 Populists are not a fringe phenomenon but the most important political force
The author says this is the most-asked question of the past decade: "Will the populist wave last, or is it about to peak?" In the summer of 2016, when Trump became the Republican nominee and Britain voted to leave the EU, the answer seemed obvious to him; now the answer is undeniable — the populists are here to stay.
