What looked abnormal a few years ago has, like it or not, become the mainstream. Populist politicians now hold power in the US, India, Turkey and much of the democratic world, and have a very high probability of taking office in France and Brazil in the coming months. Even where they remain in opposition, they are already strong enough to destroy any sense of business as usual.

0:00 The rise of one extremist party is feeding another
In the Berlin state election, Die Linke took 26% of the vote and emerged the big winner. The party descends from the SED, which ruled East Germany with an iron fist, and after reunification initially appealed mainly to older voters nostalgic for the security of the communist system; in recent years it has remade itself in the image of the global illiberal left, which the author considers roughly comparable to Zack Polanski's Greens in Britain or the more extreme parts of the DSA in the US. During the campaign, some of its supporters were filmed chanting "Yalla, Yalla Intifada!"; on election night, the head of a notorious crime family visited the party's election party and cheerfully told the media he felt an affinity with it. The party's leader will very likely now become the next mayor of Berlin — the first time an heir to the SED takes power in the capital.

0:00 Voters under 35 have swung to the two extremes
Another notable feature of the two elections is the age distribution. The SPD and CDU, which once dominated Germany's political landscape, now draw most of their support from pensioners. Among voters under 35, Die Linke and the AfD hold unassailable majorities in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. From this the author concludes that the tilt toward the extremes will only grow larger in the coming years. It also explains why the collapse of the centre is not a one-off election accident: the structure of the electorate itself is pushing the scales toward the two ends.

0:00 Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's left coalition is just an election accident
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, because a batch of other parties all failed to clear the 5% threshold for entering parliament, a broad left coalition just barely won enough votes to govern. But the author stresses that this is an election accident unlikely to repeat — a few thousand votes either way and the state would be completely ungovernable. The point matters: when centrist parties fall below the threshold, they don't just lose their own seats, they push the governability of the entire state to the edge of a cliff.

0:00 Don't surrender, and don't deny the problem is real
The author explicitly rejects two responses. The first is to urge the centre to surrender: if the political centre can't hold, then moderates might as well defect to the extremists on "their own side." He thinks this is wrong — neither Die Linke nor the AfD can solve the real problems Germany faces, and despite their enormous differences they share conspicuous similarities, from their ambiguity toward Moscow to their persistent inability to purge antisemites from their own ranks. The second is to keep denying reality: for a decade the centre has attributed the extremists' success to foreign interference, social media algorithms, some candidate's tactical blunder, or the stupidity, sexism or racism of voters. The author says these ways of blinding yourself to the facts in front of you may be comforting, but they are equally dangerous.

item.title: Going global: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and the US — go there first so you can get big
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.description: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and the US once they're big, but it's exactly backwards — you go there in order to get big. Pick the wrong region and nothing that follows — product 3.0, the channel pyramid — can be built.
item.content:encoded:
Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and the US once they're big, but it's exactly backwards — you go there in order to get big. Pick the wrong region and nothing that follows — product 3.0, the channel pyramid — can be built.

Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas-investing experience into four choices, each counterintuitive but backed by cases and numbers; the back half on AI rebuilding organisations and pricing is the densest.

1:30 The old cross-border mega-seller playbook is dead
Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border mega-seller’ model popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-style mindset — dozens or hundreds of accounts at a time; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. Ten years ago these companies made money faster than other paths, and plenty of investors loved them. But a distribution-style company is essentially a traffic-style company: the more stores, the more likely you are to get traffic. When a platform's goods aren't plentiful enough, he doesn't object to distribution; once goods are plentiful enough, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, there are three red lines: goods not matching the listing harms consumers, brushing orders harms other merchants, and slipping in little cards to build private-domain traffic harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel cares enormously about consumer experience, and these behaviours run straight into that wall.

4:38 Of the four choices, region comes first
Wei Zhe says it isn't just cross-border e-commerce — all of life is about choice mattering more than effort. He gives four choices: region, channel, product category, brand positioning. On region he has always argued for seizing the European and American market first, because paying power is strong, internet penetration is high, and more importantly a brand can build momentum there. This isn't something they invented — when Japanese and Korean brands went global back then, they all seized Europe and the US. On category they change their advice every three years: the first three years they backed products common to China and abroad, where the domestic supply chain could sell overseas without modification — Anker's power banks, for instance, were almost identical back then apart from the voltage; the second three years they advised overseas-specific products, because China's supply chain had all gone overseas and China-abroad commonality offered no differentiation; the last three years it's product 3.0 — electrified, chipped, algorithmic.

12:29 You don't go to Europe and the US after getting big — you get big by going there
Many companies tell Wei Zhe ‘I'll go to Europe and the US once I'm big’, and he says it's exactly backwards: you go to Europe and the US in order to get big. He cites Cupshe, the swimwear company — a husband and wife, 50,000 dollars of inventory, and their first stop was the US. Fifty thousand dollars is sales inventory, actually very little, so there's no real minimum threshold. Looking recently at AI smart hardware, they start from a thousand or ten thousand products on the Kickstarter crowdfunding platform, even taking prepayment before placing orders, with no capital — that's a great way to test the water. He even advises big companies entering the European and American market to learn from small startups. They always say the needle has to be fine enough to pierce through, and both big and small companies should first nail the four singles: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

20:36 After AI, good companies don't just find demand — they create it
Wei Zhe says that with AI, excellent companies don't go looking for demand; they should lead demand and create demand. He cites a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: it used to be unpowered, and they electrified it, adding a chip and an algorithm — the algorithm is actually simple, with GPS positioning, since the movements of the sky follow rules. He wasn't an astronomy hobbyist before but he'd buy one: at home in Silicon Valley you tap once, it automatically aligns Orion for you, tells you three in the morning is the best time, you set it and go to sleep, and the next day it has the shot ready for you. That lets anyone become a good astronomy hobbyist. Another example: a cross-border class student doing curtains — electrified, they didn't sell well in the US because American electricians are expensive, so he put a solar panel on the window and turned electric curtains that needed an electrician into something you can DIY; revenue went from one or two hundred million to four or five hundred million, with profit of one or two hundred million.

24:48 Still charging subscriptions in the AI era means you're behind
Wei Zhe says that in the AI era, still thinking in terms of subscription fees means you're behind again; they're all urging companies toward back-end charging, software charging — what they call tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest approach, a bit like advertising that used to charge by time rather than by usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks of vacation this month, aren't you wasting two weeks of the subscription? They advise that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not go back to the old SaaS model of 9.99 dollars a month. One AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and charges nothing if you don't read; the same for smart bike trainers — you top up, then one dollar per ride, two dollars for two hours.

27:28 Adding AI beats AI-plus, and it's the more promising bet
Wei Zhe has a formulation: AI-plus or plus-AI. He flips the phrase around — what he favours more is plus-AI, not today's AI-plus. The difference: plus-AI takes hardware humans have already accepted and makes it AI; rather than using AI to create hardware nobody has seen before. It's very hard for humans to accept entirely new hardware. Take Oura making a ring — you accepted rings first; something that hangs a camera under your neck is harder for me, I've never accepted that hardware. So they're very bullish on adding AI to already-accepted hardware. One capacitive stylus they invested in is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad — it doesn't add another pen for you, it just makes your pen AI. He also particularly wants to transform one of the top one or two overseas fitness-equipment companies, replacing the fitness instructor on the screen with an AI-generated one — you want a man, it's a man; you want a Black instructor, it's a Black instructor; install two cameras and it can coach your workout with AI.

29:43 Channels aren't laid out flat — they're a pyramid
Wei Zhe says channels aren't many channels and many roads, each parallel or even competing with the others; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and rules about which channel a new product launches in first. What counts as a light-goods channel, what counts as the main waist channel for volume — the pyramid design differs by category and by brand. He cites Anker: making power banks and mecha gear seems a bit low, so to enter the high ground of consumer electronics, the Soundcore headphones have to get into Apple flagship stores — whether it really sells a lot doesn't matter, but it can transform the brand, and Apple is the tip of the pyramid. Pop Mart must open on London's Oxford Street — even if it doesn't make money, how much can it lose? — but it has to hold that position. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels for selling goods, which definitely won't work: AliExpress is a light-goods channel, somewhere to dump stock after Amazon delists you; you can't sell on Amazon and here too, and consumers get confused.

36:14 R&D is the 1, marketing is the 0
Wei Zhe says he really dislikes throwing money at marketing. Many Chinese brands going overseas, or cross-border e-commerce companies, are very willing to add 2% of revenue as marketing expense, and consumers don't actually get it. He says: do you dare add 2% of revenue as R&D expense? He has met many bosses at the one or two billion scale; at one billion they say 20 million for R&D, and I don't know what for. He says, see, there's the problem — you don't know what for. Your 2% thrown at marketing expense makes the platform happy and consumers get nothing; but 2% thrown into R&D, consumers get it. He has always firmly believed a good product speaks for itself, and marketing is just — your R&D is the 1, marketing is the 0; if your thing is good you can amplify it, and if you don't have that 1, whatever you do, don't put on a lot of 0s. He gives three signals for judging: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and crush it by doubling its performance; second, you sell at the same price as it does; third, you sell online and it pushes offline channels to come find you.

item.title: The AI office hype hasn't cleared, and the personal Agent war has already begun | Breaking down Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.description: Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.
item.content:encoded:
Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.

Four frontline product people break down four routes — Town, Instinct, Grok Bot, Muse — and also explain why that batch of products like Xiaolongxia became martyrs. Information density is high, but the second half is worth more.

0:00 100,000 users support a $10 billion valuation
Instinct only began small-scale invite testing in February this year, and by the end of August it still hadn't reached 100,000 users, yet its valuation rose from $50 million at the start of the year to $500 million in August, $2.5 billion at the end of August, and this month the new round being circulated in the market has already reached $10 billion, with Sequoia and Benchmark both in talks to lead. The founder is a 23-year-old unknown with no big-company experience, no technical patents, no industry background. Pan Luan (潘乱) put it bluntly: what capital is buying is neither the founder nor the product, it's the story of the next OpenAI, and it can pay the price of the next-generation personal operating system to grab a ticket.

15:16 The line between tool and person is proactivity
The biggest difference between this wave of Agents and the last is that it is no longer another tool, but a person. Two differences between a person and a tool: first, long-term understanding — a tool needs the context explained again every time, while a person understands what kind of person you are like a friend or colleague; second, proactivity — setting up automated tasks in Manus still depends on prompts, on you spelling out the rules and intent, and that isn't proactivity. True proactivity is subjective initiative — like the colleague who understands your goal in doing something and comes over on their own to say, "I have a plan, should we discuss it?"

18:09 Office Agents organize by project, personal Agents organize by person
The core difference is the dimension along which context is built. Cloud Code builds context along a mission or project dimension, and switching to the next project means starting over; this wave of personal agents builds context centered on you as a person, knowing your profile, preferences and past history. Open Codex or Manus and the list on the left is all the tasks and projects you've sent out; open Grok Bot and beside you are AI companions you can drive together. In personal scenarios people care less about model capability and the harness layer, because individuals don't have that many complex tasks; office Agents are the ones that care a lot about task completion rate.

30:28 Town first trades email for the user's right to delegate
The four products are trying to solve the same problem, just with different approaches. Town has a mobile app, but 70% of its data traffic is on PC; it focuses on the email scenario, solving one high-frequency scenario well before expanding. It understands which emails you send and receive often, auto-archives, learns your writing style, drafts replies for you, and sends automatically after you click confirm. It goes deeper in the email scenario than any other agent, and overseas it has already achieved fairly viral spread, especially in school-related scenarios. In one sentence: use a high-frequency scenario to build user trust, and bit by bit acquire the user's ultimate right to delegate.

39:33 Poke didn't break out, and it wasn't a technical limit
Poke and Instinct are both agents that live inside IM and don't make a standalone app, but Poke didn't break out. Suki believes it wasn't a technical limit — Browser Use was already very mature by the end of last year, and Poke could have done it completely at the time; the difference was team strategy: Instinct went deeper in the agent direction, taking the full-delegation route, able to connect to credit cards, screen and microphone, booking flights and buying things for you — things users had never seen, which produced viral spread; Poke put its energy into content push accuracy, taking the proactive-push route, with email notifications arriving even earlier than the inbox itself, but it didn't take the step of "finishing the thing for you."

42:39 Cloud Agents have to handle three environments
Mark says doing cloud agents was a painful lesson: a local agent and a cloud agent are completely different things. To do personal AI you have to be usable anytime, anywhere — you can't be unreachable just because the computer screen is off. The cloud has to handle three environments — the user's device, the cloud service, and the agent's execution environment — and task state, task interruption and recovery, and context passing between the three are very complex systems. They started in February, and just getting the agent to run stably in the cloud took at least two months; setting aside detours, polishing a sincere piece of work takes at least three to four months.

50:39 Hiring an assistant and being a middleman are two different businesses
Town started out doing corporate tax filing, and after pivoting it leans more toward enterprise scenarios; the relationship is more like you paying to hire a personal assistant, which naturally filters for people willing to pay, with a typical profile of white-collar workers who are extremely busy and have no time or energy. Muse is more like a middleman, shopping guide or broker: although it has a paid subscription, the main projected revenue source is still commission from matching transactions, leaning toward mass users and blending into everyday WhatsApp chats. Two completely different logics, cutting different scenarios and filtering out different users.

1:14:07 For an Agent, the saved-items folder may be noise
The story Zuckerberg told when launching Muse was extracting what you like to eat from ingredients saved on Instagram, generating a shopping list, adjusting the menu by dinner party size and dietary restrictions, then completing the shopping and relationship maintenance — turning years of interest profile into money, going from a discovery platform to a decision and transaction platform. But Suki suspects this is to save face for the free business narrative: helping users complete transactions is absolutely not among the top scenarios users want to solve; users more want to solve the annoying things they don't want to do themselves. There isn't that much high-quality context in saved-items folders; truly high-quality context comes more from offline, IM and email, and Douyin and Instagram saves may themselves be noise to an agent.

item.title: Ten Years of Parenting Taught Me: When Your Kid Won't Listen, the Problem Isn't Your Kid
