item.description: The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue halves.
item.content:encoded:
The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue halves.

Regulation, stablecoins, Circle Arc, the Meta vs Instinct fight, Polymarket's talent war — high information density, and the second half is worth more than the first.

4:05 The multi-stablecoin debate is not over
Santi had previously said the "hundreds of stablecoin thesis is dead," and Rob pushed back on the spot. Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins; SoFi, Verve, two bank consortia, the Stripe consortium, MoneyGram, and Western Union are all doing it, and Bridge already has its own stablecoin internally for treasury management. His mechanism: big companies hold a lot of cash, and if they can earn yield on it, they have an incentive to issue their own coin rather than use USDC or USDT. Santi pressed: don't these big companies have FX desks at JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley? Rob said it depends on the company's size and the complexity of global treasury management — Western Union's remittance corridors in Africa and Latin America are something JP Morgan's correspondent banking network can't do well.

13:18 CLARITY failed, but nobody has really given up
The Senate voted down the CLARITY Act 49 to 50 on Tuesday; it needed 60 votes. Three Republicans — Susan Collins, Josh Hawley, and Jerry Moran — voted against, and every Democrat they had been counting on voted against. Santi said not to overread Tillis's turn, noting Kirsten Gillibrand said that same day she is still pushing the legislation. On Polymarket the odds of passage briefly fell to 4%, then recovered to 8%. Markets fell on the news, with Coinbase down 10% and Circle down 12%. Rob said it's worth remembering that dozens of people worked on this bill for a year, including staff on the Banking Committee and the Agriculture Committee.

16:58 The SEC gives tokenized stocks a five-year exemption
The SEC issued an order granting tokenized securities trading venues (TSVS) a five-year interim conditional exemption, letting them trade tokenized NMS stocks using permissioned AMMs and liquidity pools without registering as exchanges, and liquidity providers got a limited market-maker exemption. Two key conditions: token holders must get the same rights as the underlying stock, such as dividends and voting; and third-party tokenization requires written notice and giving the issuer a chance to object. Santi read that out and said this clause could directly break the current onchain tokenized stock practice — if AMC can object, you can't just throw AMC onto Hyperliquid. Rob said this is almost certainly coming, because onchain tokenized stocks currently create strange dislocations after hours and pre-market, and Robinhood pairing memecoins with tokenized stocks is an example.

22:43 The tokenization winner is the whole ecosystem
Rob said it's hard to point to a single winner. The obvious beneficiaries are issuers, existing exchanges and clearinghouses, new exchanges that want into the US market (Coinbase, Polymarket, Lighter, Hyperliquid, Backpack), global neobanks, and new transfer agents and core infrastructure providers like Alpaca. Santi said his first reaction was Superstate and Securitize, and Securitize rose 16% that day. Rob said this is more a rising tide lifting all boats than value concentrating in one place. He added that as more assets go onchain, everything onchain gets bigger — more liquidity, more users, better infrastructure, more stablecoin issuance.

29:06 S&P buying Open Zeppelin is buying data
S&P is a ratings agency with a roughly $120 billion market cap and about $14 billion in revenue. This week it first led Kao's Series B extension (Kao raised its Series B four years ago; this time it may have raised about $50 million, bringing the total Series B to about $110 million, with investors including RBC, DRW, Broadridge, BNP, and Nasdaq), then acquired smart contract security firm Open Zeppelin. Rob said the acquisition surprised him; Open Zeppelin doesn't seem like a company that would run a process to sell itself. His read: S&P gives ratings, and it can use Open Zeppelin for real-time risk benchmarks and data, to assess what's happening in protocols, and then sell that to clients. Santi said he heard this is the first such deal, and there will be more from traditional capital markets data and analytics players like Moody's. Rob said many crypto companies raised a lot of money and have good products but aren't good enough as standalone businesses, and companies like S&P grow into conglomerates by constantly buying good niche products and then bundling them for you through a terminal.

37:40 Circle pushing memes on Arc's first day was a misstep
Circle launched Arc, with more than 190 partners on day one and over $220 million in TVL pre-seeded in a Morpho vault. Rob said he doesn't understand why Circle came out on day one pushing a bunch of memes, since Arc had always been positioned as a payments-first chain, talking about agentic finance, privacy, FX liquidity, and real business activity. He said this is the exact opposite of the story Circle has long told, and it left a lot of people with a bad impression. Santi said he went to Circle's launch event yesterday, and the room and Twitter were two completely different worlds — within an hour he met people from BlackRock, DTCC, ICE, Visa, and MoneyGram, and Circle's convening power is extremely strong; if it had launched purely on its original positioning, the effect would have been much better. Rob said Circle may have seen Robinhood chain's success, but Robinhood is a trading platform and Circle is a payments company, and having bought Taza Pay it should stay in its lane.

42:38 Circle's revenue gets cut in half by rates
Rob said he doesn't expect 4% to 4.5% rates to last forever, and that rates will normalize to between 2% and 3%, which means if Circle is just an interest income business, its revenue at current TVL would halve. He also said that as a payments stablecoin, if you can't share yield with end customers, there isn't much reason to hold large amounts of it. Circle's agreement with Coinbase requires giving 50% to Coinbase, which puts it at a disadvantage competing with new stablecoins. So Circle is trying to become a payments company and get a payments company multiple, and Arc and Circle Payment Network are part of that story. Santi said don't underestimate USDC's network effect — in DeFi there is now only one thing that matters for liquidity, and that's USDC; any DeFi founder needs USDC on their platform.

46:14 Instinct's reckoning comes in month four
Rob said companies are now getting bigger faster and raising more money faster, that venture capital as a market structure is broken, and that the hottest companies see valuations rise faster and faster regardless of fundamentals. He said a company's first big reckoning usually comes in year four, but Instinct's first big reckoning will come in month four — because the two biggest companies in the world are about to launch direct competitors, Grokbot and Meta's Muse. Santi said from his own use Muse is six to eight times better than Instinct; Instinct is clearly compute-constrained, and for the same question Muse is sometimes 10 to 15 minutes faster, fails less, and can route around the roadblocks Resy set up for these products. Rob said he doesn't know how growth investors are comfortable at this valuation, and the only thing that could prove them wrong is Instinct sprinting to train its own model, but that requires a billion dollars to build data centers.

item.title: Prediction Markets Aren't Casinos, but 90% of the Volume Is Sports
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.description: Kalshi traded four years of compliance for 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a bookmaker's; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.
item.content:encoded:
Kalshi traded four years of compliance for 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a bookmaker's; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.

The first half is founder narrative; the value is in the middle and back: how contracts are written, sports at 90%, regulatory risk. Worth listening for anyone who wants to understand the mechanics of prediction markets.

8:16 Comply for four years first, then open the first market
Kalshi's two founders wrote "regulatory first" into the company's principles and spent four years getting regulatory approval before launching their first market. Mansoor calls this anti-Silicon Valley: others build the product and patch in compliance later, whereas they first asked the federal government how the thing should be regulated. The cost was that for the first four years they thought about quitting almost every day, held up by the fact that the cost of regret would be too high. The payoff came in 2024, when a federal appeals court ruled Kalshi could list election contracts, landing before the presidential election. Mansoor attributes the 90% market share directly to that path: institutions would rather plug into a platform inside the system, because changing the rules from outside the system is harder.

15:36 Prediction markets force you to shut up, not to take a position
Robin Hanson lays out three mechanisms that make prediction markets more accurate than polls or expert interviews. First, people being interviewed have an incentive to be interesting, dramatic and to please the questioner, while the market only rewards being right. Second, the market gives you an incentive to shut up about topics you don't understand — you only bet in the few markets where you genuinely have an edge, whereas interviewees will answer anyway. Third, the market doesn't require you to have a direct opinion on a topic; it invites you to find the biases and errors in other people's pricing, and pays you to correct them. He closes with the old poker-table line: sit down and look for the sucker; if you can't find him, the sucker is you, so don't play that market.

20:48 Internal prediction markets die on the project owner's excuse
Eli Lilly ran an internal prediction market in the early 2000s that successfully predicted which drug compounds would pass Phase III trials; Google ran one called Google Profit. Both were judged effective, and neither survived. Hanson's explanation: the project owner wants to know whether they'll deliver on time, but what they want even more is a good excuse if they fail. And the best excuse is precisely "everything was going fine and then at the last minute something nobody could have foreseen happened." A market that keeps accurately predicting whether you'll be late voids that excuse in advance, so nobody wants it to exist.

22:58 Domain expertise is not the key ability for forecasting the future
Mansoor cites Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting research: put experts in a given domain, say geopolitics, up against a group of non-experts forecasting the same set of events, and the non-experts win. His explanation is that domain experts become too doctrinaire over time, while people who can step back and look at a problem coolly are better calibrated and less biased. Mansoor says this is a fairly heretical statement in politics, academia and financial analysis — it implies that if you want a more accurate answer, you should look for a diverse group of participants who pride themselves on self-calibration, critical reading and filtering information, not an authority in some field. He treats this as Kalshi's underlying logic.

33:28 One contract takes a month to write, for grammar and apostrophes
Nicole Kagan writes the contracts and self-certifies them with the CFTC. The most complex category is "what someone will say in a given speech," and they recently rewrote the rules because a pile of grammar problems came up: what if there's an apostrophe? If the word is said wrong, or pronounced wrong, does it still count as the same word? What if it appears inside a proper noun? What if the livestream cuts out midway and the clip is uploaded somewhere else later? Those rules took more than a month to write, seven or eight pages, extremely detailed. When Bloomberg reported on it, they guessed the rules were for automated processing and must be for AI; Kagan says that's not it at all — they wrote them so users could understand, and never considered that what a human can understand a computer can probably understand too.

35:35 When you can't call it, settle at the last fair price
Kalshi's contracts are usually binary: pay $1 if the event happens, $0 if it doesn't, with every position fully collateralized — if one side bets 30 cents, someone must bet 70 cents. But some situations can't be judged yes or no. Cardi B was clearly dancing during her seven-second shot in the Super Bowl halftime show, but she had no mic and there was no way to confirm whether she was singing, so the team said "we are epistemologically uncertain" and settled at the last fair price. Another case is 50-50: when multiple people win at once, each settles at 50 cents. Kagan says they have the right to do this when it is genuinely unclear whether an event meets the criteria, and they have already revised the halftime show contract — the new rules require an audible lead or backing vocal, and under the new rules Cardi B counts as not having performed.

41:52 Ninety percent of volume comes from sports, and that's the most uncomfortable fact
Dubner puts it bluntly: roughly 90% of Kalshi's volume is concentrated in a category barely mentioned until then — sports, the business that makes DraftKings and FanDuel nervous. Mansoor's response is that the sports share is falling fast and other categories are growing faster, but he concedes that "10% is also a lot, don't forget we're very large." He insists on distinguishing gambling from trading: all derivatives markets are mostly speculative, speculation provides liquidity, and the key isn't whether there's speculation but the business model — one model specifically hunts for losers and bans winners, the other pursues price discovery and wants smart people in. He also concedes the second model carries risk, saying there is "responsible gambling" and "responsible trading," and that platforms have a responsibility to monitor.

44:00 Seventy to eighty percent of active users never place an order
Mansoor says one of his favorite numbers is that 70% to 80% of active users don't trade; they just log in every day, keep it next to X and a few newspapers, and use it to calibrate or check information. Kalshi's business model is a neutral platform, like the NYSE or Nasdaq, taking an average 1% on trades and not caring who wins or loses. He also says the information environment is becoming more polarized and the signal-to-noise ratio is falling, because social media algorithms reward clickbait: write a nuanced, restrained, multi-paragraph take on X and you get four likes; write something extreme and outrageous and you get tens of thousands. Prediction markets have exactly the opposite incentive — that nuanced, boring, well-calibrated judgment is the one that makes money.

item.title: Diffusion Isn't Just for Images — It's Going to Win at Language Model Inference
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.description: Autoregressive inference must generate one token at a time, sequentially, and is memory-bandwidth bound; diffusion models process many tokens in parallel, so the inference workload looks more like training — which is why Inception is betting on it.
item.content:encoded:
Autoregressive inference must generate one token at a time, sequentially, and is memory-bandwidth bound; diffusion models process many tokens in parallel, so the inference workload looks more like training — which is why Inception is betting on it.

A diffusion model founder explains clearly why parallelism at inference becomes the architectural deciding factor, and how a 50-person company finds differentiation in the gap between giants.

3:10 Diffusion started because GANs were too unstable
Ermon says that when he was working on image generation back then, he was very dissatisfied with GANs: they worked, but training was extremely unstable and results were hard to reproduce. So in 2019 he and his PhD students turned to score-based generative models, with the idea of training a neural network to denoise — if it can denoise, that means it understands image structure, and it can then work in reverse to progressively refine a clean image out of pure noise. This is the underlying technology of modern diffusion models. He stresses that today's best image, video, some music, and a large number of protein models are all based on diffusion.

5:11 The 2024 paper moved diffusion onto text
Ermon's team published a paper in 2024 that, for the first time at GPT-2 scale (under a billion parameters), got a diffusion model to match autoregressive model quality: the same perplexity, the same degree of data fit, but roughly 10x faster generation, because diffusion outputs multiple tokens at once. He says this was still fairly academic, but it was enough to make him decide to start a company and scale the technology to commercial size.

8:14 Autoregressive inference is a memory bandwidth bottleneck
Ermon likens the 2017 switch from RNNs to transformers to the inference stage: during training, transformers won by processing multiple tokens in parallel, but at inference time autoregressive models are still sequential — before generating the 10th token you must first generate all the preceding tokens. This workload is extremely memory-bandwidth limited; most of the time is spent moving weights between levels of the memory hierarchy, with very little arithmetic, which is unfriendly to GPUs. Diffusion models' inference workload looks more like training — processing multiple tokens in parallel at once — so it naturally matches the compute pattern GPUs are good at.

10:16 Inference efficiency also caps RL post-training
Ermon points out that economics are determined by how much intelligence you get per watt and per dollar. Much of the progress in reasoning models comes from test-time compute scaling, and one of the bottlenecks in RL post-training is generating rollouts — letting the model explore, scoring trajectories, then improving the model. So inference efficiency directly gates post-training efficiency: a model that scales better at inference will automatically also scale better during post-training. This is the core logic behind his bet on diffusion LLMs, and what he means by ‘more parallel approaches will eventually win’.

12:19 Mercury is benchmarked against Haiku, Flash, mini
Ermon says Inception's Mercury model is benchmarked against speed-optimized models like Haiku, Flash, and the mini nano series, with comparable quality but significantly faster, and it is already serving customers in production. He stresses that you cannot run a diffusion LLM directly on vLLM or SGLang — you have to build your own serving engine to handle the complexity of real production workloads. This is both a barrier and a moat: even if someone else trains a diffusion LLM, without a corresponding serving engine they can't put it to use.

17:21 A voice customer switched from custom chips back to Nvidia GPUs
Ermon gives the example of voice agent company OpenCall: the voice pipeline includes ASR, an inference LLM for tool calling, and TTS, and speed is critical. OpenCall originally served the LLM on Cerebras custom chips to reach the required speed, then switched to Inception's diffusion LLM, because it could get the same speed on Nvidia GPUs — higher availability, lower cost, better quality. Ermon says once you get used to a fast model you can't go back, like broadband.

25:26 Diffusion is inherently more controllable than autoregression
Ermon says diffusion models are generally easier to control than autoregressive models: autoregression must wait until the entire object is generated before you know whether it satisfies constraints, whether it is aligned, what score the reward function gives it; diffusion generates coarse-to-fine, so from early on you can judge whether the direction is right, and you can use external reward functions or constraint sets to guide generation. There is a fair amount of evidence in the academic literature supporting this, and some guidance methods simply cannot be done on autoregressive models. He sees this as the differentiation space for future product experiences.

29:29 20% to 30% of tasks are extremely latency-sensitive
Ermon estimates based on OpenRouter's task categories (research, chat, coding, software engineering, log processing, etc.) that about 20% to 30% of those tasks care a great deal about latency. As a lower bound, that portion of the workload can be served by whichever model provides the highest quality within a given latency budget. He also acknowledges that we are not yet at frontier intelligence levels, and much of the workload still requires frontier-level intelligence, so the addressable market for diffusion models is layered.

item.title: When Your Kids Fight, Are You a Witness or a Judge
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-你是证人还是法官/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-你是证人还是法官/
item.description: The mistake parents most often make when stepping into sibling conflict is refereeing with their own childhood fairness wounds. What kids need isn't a verdict on who was right, but practice repairing a relationship inside low-stakes conflict.
item.content:encoded:
The mistake parents most often make when stepping into sibling conflict is refereeing with their own childhood fairness wounds. What kids need isn't a verdict on who was right, but practice repairing a relationship inside low-stakes conflict.

Medium information density with a clear core framework: witness not judge, sportscaster mode, fair is not equal. Suited to parents of more than one child, especially those whose own childhood emotions get triggered by sibling fights.

3:05 Deal with your own sibling baggage before you step in
The episode opens by pointing out that almost everyone carries sibling baggage — even without siblings, there's either a longing for that ‘mythic connection’ or relief at not having it. The fairness trap is the thing most likely to trigger a parent's emotions: a cake sliced unevenly, a rule that was looser for one kid, a new dress given to only one of them — those memories get activated the moment you see your own kids fighting. If you step in before dealing with that baggage, you are effectively imposing your sibling history on your children. So the first step is always clearing your own head, not rushing in to hand down a verdict.

4:07 You are a witness, not a judge
This is the single most important line in the whole piece, and Dr. Pressman repeats it a dozen-plus times. The moment you start deciding who was right, who hit first, who was worse, that judgment comes from your own history, not from what actually happened between these two children in front of you. As a witness, your job is to observe and describe, not to rule. That distinction determines your tone, your words and your posture when you step in. Once you become the judge, you will unconsciously favor, convict and punish — and what the kids feel isn't justice, it's your unfinished childhood emotions making decisions for them.

5:09 When you must step in
Dr. Pressman gives clear signals for intervening: a child is in danger, there's a power imbalance, or they're stuck in a loop they can't get out of. If the two are evenly matched and physically safe, you can stay nearby and occasionally ask ‘Is everyone okay?’ But watch especially for power dynamics turning into toxic bullying — rare, but when it happens an adult must cut it off. Kids who experience peer or sibling bullying have far worse adult outcomes, and the damage is much bigger than we realize. Bullying, though, has a strict definition: a power difference plus repeated, malicious, intentional abuse. Merely ‘being a jerk’ isn't bullying, and kids being jerks to each other is completely normal.

6:17 Sportscaster mode: describe, don't adjudicate
If you do need to step in, Dr. Pressman recommends ‘sportscaster mode’ — you act like an observant, reflective commentator who simply describes what happened. For example: ‘I noticed this happened over here, and that happened over there — did I get that right?’ This lets you validate both children at once, without taking sides, without a winner. The key is avoiding questions like ‘Who started it?’ ‘You always do this’ ‘There's something wrong with you.’ When you tell a child there's something wrong with who they are rather than with a behavior, you're feeding the exact habit you don't want them using on each other — turning anger and outbursts into a judgment of a person's worth. ‘You're stupid’ says ‘you are a stupid person,’ and no one needs to hear that.

8:21 Stop dehumanizing language on the spot
Dr. Pressman says kids can scream, yell, be vicious to each other, even get physical — but if she hears dehumanizing language, she pauses the fight right there to change the wording. Because what you want to constantly ‘wire’ and ‘bake’ into your kids is: talk about the behavior, not about who the person is. This isn't a lesson afterward, it's immediate intervention. She'll say ‘Let's rephrase that’ in the moment. The logic: language habits need repeated reinforcement to internalize, and every dehumanizing expression you let slide reinforces the opposite.

14:33 Fair is not equal — it's needs-based
Dr. Pressman uses the peanut butter cupcake example to explain the difference between fair and equal: giving two kids peanut butter cupcakes of identical size and identical recipe looks equal, but if one of them is allergic to peanuts, it's completely unfair. Fair means giving each child what they need, not giving everyone the same thing. This framework protects you when a child demands ‘Why does my 12-year-old sister have a phone and I don't?’ — you can answer ‘You're different people, I've learned more since then, and I'm making a different decision that's better for you.’ If you try to be perfectly equal, you're assuming every child is the same age, the same temperament, the same personality, the same interests, the same needs — which obviously doesn't hold.

16:37 Don't label your kids
Dr. Pressman points out that giving all your kids the same label (say, ‘you're all helpers’) does promote positive behavior, but labeling only one child in the family as ‘the helper’ creates tension and problematic dynamics. Labels plant seeds of resentment, insecurity and lack of motivation, and push siblings apart. Teachers, friends, other parents, relatives will all label your kids; a parent's job is to counteract that damage, not join in. Labels ‘haunt’ a child — Dr. Pressman uses the word haunt, and says it sounds dramatic but it's true.

18:41 Repair is not a forced apology
Dr. Pressman distinguishes real repair from fake repair. Repair isn't necessarily a public apology — if the kids finish fighting and suddenly giggle together, share an inside joke, make faces at each other, that is repair, that is reconnection, and you're watching it happen. Every reconnection strengthens the relationship and tells your kids ‘this relationship is forever, it gets messy, but we always come back.’ But a forced apology is not repair. Saying ‘sorry’ and saying ‘apologize to your brother’ don't teach what the research literature calls repair. An insincere apology only makes people angrier. You can ask ‘How do you think that made your sibling feel? Is there anything you could do to help them feel better?’ If the child says no, you don't just drop it — you come back later and ask ‘Have you had time to think about that?’

item.title: America's Richest Are Hiding in Small Business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-oddlots-美国最富的一群人-藏在小生意里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-oddlots-美国最富的一群人-藏在小生意里/
item.description: Half of the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income, and the owners of these businesses are not tech giants — they are car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.
item.content:encoded:
Half of the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income, and the owners of these businesses are not tech giants — they are car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.

New research built on linked IRS full tax-return data pulls the question of "who the rich are" away from the tech narrative and back to regional middle-market businesses; high information density, suited to anyone tracking taxes, PE and wealth distribution.

6:13 Tax returns assemble a different picture of the rich
More than a decade ago the two authors were commissioned by the Treasury to link corporate tax returns with the returns of owners and employees, because even the IRS could not match the different forms belonging to the same business. They found that the picture of the rich painted by the media and by Capital in the Twenty-First Century is very different from the actual picture in US tax returns: not passive rent-collecting Gilded Age monopolists, but millions of actively operating middle-market regional business owners. That data project later became the basis of the book.

12:16 Seventy percent of pass-through income flows to the top 1%
Of pass-through business income, 70 cents of every dollar flows to the top 1% of earners. From the 1980s to 2021, more than half of the rise in the top 1%'s income share came from pass-through business income. So anyone trying to understand income inequality and wealth inequality cannot get around this sector. The authors originally assumed monopolistic giants were passively collecting the money, but found instead middle-market regional businesses spread across the whole country, numbering in the millions.

15:22 Car dealers are the single biggest bucket of pass-through income
The book opens with a "wedding of the century": a third-generation Mercedes dealer in Florida held his daughter's wedding in Paris, rented out Versailles for the dinner, and spent $60 million — right after selling the dealership for several hundred million dollars. Looking at top 0.1% pass-through income by industry, the authors found car dealers ranked first. They then checked yacht and private jet registration data and found these people by name, because tax returns themselves cannot identify individuals.

19:23 A car dealer's wealth is half skill, half licence
The authors tell two stories. Larry Miller started in Toyota's parts division, took the parts business from 961st to first, later owned more than 40 dealerships and bought the Utah Jazz — a good case of "move slow and make things". But the other side is regulatory protection: franchise laws were meant to protect small dealers from being force-fed inventory by Ford and GM, yet in 2008 Chrysler had three times as many dealerships as Toyota while selling the same number of cars, and closing a store meant paying three years' rent. Dealers also enjoy geographic monopolies and high margins on add-on services like warranties and financing.

22:25 Beer distributors are a rent-collecting layer left by Prohibition
The truck you see on the road with Budweiser on it actually belongs to a distributor, such as Reyes. These distributors sit between brewers and bars, restaurants and grocery stores; state laws require beer to pass through this layer, originally to stop big brewers from controlling production and distribution at the same time. The result is that these "little guys" became big guys, showing up in large numbers in the private jet data. The authors mention a beer wholesalers' convention in San Antonio where the mayor said he had never seen so many private jets at the airport.

34:31 Same anaesthesiologist, far higher tax burden for the employee
The book contrasts two anaesthesiologists: one runs a private practice through an S-Corp, the other draws a salary from a hospital system. The former treats most of his income as business profit, pays no payroll tax and no uncapped Medicare surtax, even though he bills Medicare heavily. The IRS only requires payroll tax on the "reasonable compensation" portion of wages; anything above that counts as profit. The 2017 reform cut the top pass-through rate from 37% to below 30%, and although it put guardrails on professional services such as doctors, carving out surgery, ancillary services or real estate still lets more income be shifted into the lower-rate bucket.

38:35 A quarter of federal elected officials are pass-through owners too
The authors say the reason the tax loophole has survived so long is that roughly a quarter of federal elected officials are themselves pass-through business owners. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno is a car dealer, and the Social Security plan he proposed together with Elizabeth Warren is funded by a payroll tax on working-class wages, with no mention at all of these wealthy business owners. The authors argue the most realistic reform is not to abolish the loophole but to cap it by income: for instance, once business income exceeds $1 million or $400,000, you can no longer claim the deduction that cuts the rate from 37% to 30%.

48:52 The owners' share of the pie rose from four tenths to five
Over the past 25 years, 60% of growth in the corporate sector came from the pass-through form, so the pie is getting bigger; at the same time, the share owners take out of the pie rose from a third to 40% to about 50%. Using data from 2001 to 2021, the authors calculate that value added per worker rose from $34,000 to $52,000, a gain of $18,000, of which owners took $15,000. They attribute this to scarce skills (the US has 30% fewer doctors per capita than the OECD average, with the AMA restricting supply), policy-created scarcity, and the rising value of professional services such as M&A.

item.content:encoded:
Altman says going public now is "unwise," citing safety; but at the same time OpenAI is negotiating a $1.2 trillion raise, and the CFO has been excluded from investor meetings.

Three Indicators of the Week segments, one number each. The OpenAI segment has real internal tension; the other two are price tracking with average information density.

2:01 US households paid $820 extra for this war
Waylon's indicator is $108 billion — the extra fuel cost US consumers have paid since the Iran war began in late February, gasoline plus diesel combined, or about $820 per US household. The figure comes from Brown University's Climate Solutions Lab, which tracks it live on its website, with the red number ticking upward. The method uses the average price over the 30 days before the war as a baseline, then adjusts for seasonality — people drive more in summer, demand is higher, prices were supposed to rise anyway. In other words, it is a counterfactual estimate of what oil would cost if this war had not happened. Diesel has already broken $6 a gallon, a record.

3:01 Diesel costs land on your Amazon order
Most Americans do not drive diesel cars, but diesel prices affect them anyway. Trucks, trains, factories and farms all run on diesel, and the extra money paid at those stages passes through to grocery prices and Amazon packages. Brown's tracker says this explicitly: higher diesel costs mean higher consumer prices, whether or not you fill up. This transmission chain is the key to understanding the fertilizer segment later — diesel and fertilizer together push food prices up.

4:07 OpenAI says no IPO while negotiating $1.2 trillion
Ricky's indicator is $1.2 trillion, the size of the latest funding round OpenAI is negotiating with private investors, according to the Financial Times. At the same time, Sam Altman told Fortune he is not preparing to take the company public, on the grounds that "given everything that's happening on the safety side, going public now would be unwise." Ricky points out the oddity directly: if the product really is unsafe, why keep building it? Earlier this year The Information reported that Altman and CFO Sarah Fryer disagreed on IPO timing — Altman wanted to go public sooner, Fryer was worried about the company's spending.

5:11 The CFO does not report to the CEO, which is itself unusual
This is the most concrete information in the whole episode. Fryer does not report to Altman — that kind of relationship between a CEO and a CFO is very unusual. Altman is also said to have excluded Fryer from some meetings with major backers, which is likewise unusual. Separately, OpenAI filed a confidential S1 in June, meaning it disclosed its finances to regulators but not to the public. Ricky's inference: if OpenAI's IPO lands and performs badly, that could be bad news for the entire stock and bond market propped up by the AI growth narrative. And if safety really is the issue, going public means being more transparent about financial health and perhaps safety records — which is why safety is the worry now.

6:11 Anthropic is still pushing ahead with its own IPO
Ricky uses a metaphor: OpenAI is like a couple that has been together ten years and still cannot decide whether to marry — you are worth a trillion dollars, it is time to grow up. Meanwhile rival Anthropic is still pushing ahead with its own IPO. Waylon chimes in that they are like Goldie Hawn and Kurt Russell — together a long time, raising kids together, never married. The conclusion: as long as OpenAI and Anthropic are happy, they do not need to go public, and they can whenever they want.

7:14 Sulfur went from $170 to $1,100 a ton
Cooper's indicator is $1,100 — roughly what it costs to buy one metric ton of sulfur. The average price over the past decade was about $170, a rise of about 500%, a whole extra zero. Sulfur is a key input for fertilizer, and fertilizer is essential for growing food. The strange part: the US produces most of its own sulfur, domestic supply is fine, but several other major supply hubs are in the Middle East, China and Russia, all places with obvious tensions. Sulfur also passes through major Middle Eastern commercial waterways — Cooper names the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, saying they are being blocked up.

8:18 The US produces its own sulfur but cannot escape global prices
This is the oil logic: even if the US is a major producer, it is not immune to global price increases. Supply falls, and the price is pushed up for everyone. The scale of the increase has already changed the economics for fertilizer producers — a company called Mosaic told them it has idled two plants in Louisiana because of insufficient sulfur supply. This is not a forecast; it is an actual impact that has already happened.

9:18 Diesel plus fertilizer means food inflation rises another 3% to 5%
Connect the previous two: diesel at record highs, plus a fertilizer shortage, leaves the agriculture industry in a bad spot. Rabobank, a bank focused on agriculture, expects US food inflation to rise another 3% to 5% next year — after already rising 4% to 6% this year. Cooper says he put that number in this week's Indicator newsletter.

item.title: Hair relaxer made Black women beautiful, and made them pay with their health
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ninepi-直发剂让黑人女性变美-也让她们付出健康代价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ninepi-直发剂让黑人女性变美-也让她们付出健康代价/
item.description: Chemical hair relaxer built the Black community's earliest millionaire industry and has also been linked by research to elevated uterine cancer risk — the same product is both an economic ladder and a bodily cost.
item.content:encoded:
Chemical hair relaxer built the Black community's earliest millionaire industry and has also been linked by research to elevated uterine cancer risk — the same product is both an economic ladder and a bodily cost.

This episode has medium information density, but it tells the story of how a single product can be empowerment and harm at once, very concretely — suited to listeners interested in consumer history, public health, and the racial economy.

1:06 Hair relaxer is "creamy crack"
Chemical hair relaxer has a nickname in the salon: creamy crack, because it is said to be as addictive as cocaine — once you start, it is very hard to stop. When you stop, the new curly growth breaks at the boundary with the already straightened dead hair. In the week before use you cannot wash your hair or scratch your scalp, or you will get burned; when applying it you have to avoid the scalp and coat only the hair shaft, but leaving it too long near the ends still stings. On the show the host recalls being slathered with relaxer for the first time at age 9, having already seen women in the salon cry out in pain.

5:18 From African hair tradition to a survival strategy
Hair historian Lorie Tharps says starting the story from slavery is starting from chapter two and missing chapter one: Africa already had rich hair traditions, and hair connected tribe, family, and identity. After being enslaved in America, straightening hair went from self-expression to survival strategy — because they were told their hair was inferior, ugly, more like an animal's, and straightening it became a visual way to prove "we are equal to you." They used butter instead of palm oil, made shampoo from cornmeal and kerosene, used butter knives as crude curling irons, and wrapped hair in yarn to straighten it.

8:21 Barbers' money built Black colleges
The methods these enslaved people invented were good enough to make them the first choice as barbers and wig makers for white people. White people paid for their craft, and this channel let many of them buy their own freedom. Tharps says some early Black colleges and institutions were funded or founded by Black barbers, such as Wilberforce University — an HBCU wholly owned and operated by African Americans, built to a large extent on barbering income. But the irony is that these Black barbers did not cut Black people's hair at the time; they served white clients.

10:22 The hot comb gives way to an accidental discovery
Madame CJ Walker and Annie Turnbo Malone used the hot comb plus hair oil to produce sleek straight hair, turning scattered straightening methods into a system, and Walker thereby became the first self-made millionaire woman in America, of any color. But the hot comb's effect was temporary, reverting with sweat, moisture, or rain. In the early 1900s, Cleveland tailor Garrett Augustus Morgan wanted to invent a substance that kept high-speed machines and needles from damaging wool and other animal fur, and after trying a formula he found the fur had straightened. He first tested it on a neighbor's dog, then on his own hair, and both straightened — he had accidentally discovered that lye (sodium hydroxide) plus other things could straighten hair.

14:24 The man who put relaxer on drugstore shelves
George Johnson is called by Tharps the Madam CJ Walker of his era. A barber who made homemade conks came to this chemist and asked whether he could make something fast and easy, and that produced Ultra Wave for men, followed by Ultra Sheen for women. Unlike the temporary hot comb and dangerous homemade lye formulas, Ultra Sheen was long-lasting, safer, and available at any drugstore, with no need to go to a salon. That privacy was crucial: straightening hair with chemicals carried shame, and doing it at home meant no one saw you going to the salon.

16:26 Profits flowed back to the Black community, then regulators took notice
Johnson put profits back into the Black community: Soul Train, Essence Magazine, Chicago's Independence Bank — then the largest Black-owned bank in the country, lending to homeowners and entrepreneurs redlined by white banks; funding Martin Luther King Jr. and Jesse Jackson; employing hundreds of Black and brown workers who could not find jobs because of racial discrimination, giving them profit sharing, full health insurance, on-site nurses, full college tuition, paid maternity and sick leave, and four-day weekends every holiday. In 1964 Johnson Products became the first Black-owned company listed on the American Stock Exchange. But in 1975 the FTC required Johnson to put a warning label on the outside of relaxer packaging, saying the product contained lye and could be harmful — while Revlon's relaxer, which also contained lye, was not immediately required to add a label, and the delay ran nearly two years.

20:28 The civil rights movement flipped the politics of straight hair
During the Black Power movement, Black people decided straight hair had solved nothing — from Madam CJ Walker's straightening comb to relaxer, every method had been tried and it still had not worked. So came a simpler and more radical idea: I will no longer straighten my hair, I will use my hair as protest. Black hair grows up and out, and it does not make you smaller, it makes you taller. The political flip was so complete that some Black people with naturally straight hair got perms to curl it, because not everyone's hair can grow into an Angela Davis-style afro. But the beauty industry then commodified the afro, selling wigs and marketing it as beauty and empowerment while also pulling its teeth, turning it into just another fashion trend. By the 1980s, straight hair was back.

28:38 A 34,000-woman study: risk up two and a half times
A large 2022 study followed 34,000 women and found that frequent users of chemical hair straightening products — most of them Black women — were two and a half times as likely to develop uterine cancer as never-users. New York Times Magazine contributor Linda Varosa says this was the first high-quality study to link straightening products, Black women, and two cancers (endometrial cancer and uterine cancer). The study also linked these products to fibroids, and Black women have fibroids at far higher rates than other women. The study shows correlation, not causation, but Tharps thinks agonizing over correlation versus causation misses the point: she thinks the red flag should simply be waved, with warnings on packaging, labels, and in salons.

item.title: A Broken Arm Forced a Perfect French Score: Constraints Are the Engine of Creativity
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-cautionary-断臂逼出的法语满分-限制才是创造力的引擎/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-cautionary-断臂逼出的法语满分-限制才是创造力的引擎/
item.description: After David Epstein broke his arm he was forced to replace note-taking with image-based memory, and his French scores went to perfect. During a two-day London Underground strike, many people found better commutes. Constraints aren't obstacles — they're the switch that forces you to experiment.
item.content:encoded:
After David Epstein broke his arm he was forced to replace note-taking with image-based memory, and his French scores went to perfect. During a two-day London Underground strike, many people found better commutes. Constraints aren't obstacles — they're the switch that forces you to experiment.

Medium information density. The core is the framework distinguishing useful constraints from useless ones; the second half on scientific integrity and startup experimentation is worth more than the first.

5:28 A broken arm forced a memory method into existence
In eighth grade, playing American football, David Epstein threw too hard and his arm snapped on the follow-through; his right arm was bound from shoulder to hand against his torso. His French class had a weekly dictation test: listen to a native speaker's recording and fill in the blanks in a text. He was mediocre. With his right hand bound, he couldn't write fast enough with his left, so he had to hold the flying words in his head first, by linking each word to something sports-related — he didn't know at the time this was called a mnemonic device. As a result he could remember every word, then slowly fill them in with his left hand, and started getting perfect scores. The key mechanism: his most convenient path was blocked, forcing him to find an alternative — and the alternative was better.

8:35 A two-day subway strike improved commutes for years
During a London Underground strike, people were forced to find different routes to work. The strike lasted only 48 hours, but a substantial share of people discovered a better commute than the one they had used for weeks, months or even years, and kept using it afterward. Epstein recalls the study saying this collectively saved about 1,500 hours of commuting per day. His inference: we normally experiment too little; useful constraints drive people to run experiments they otherwise wouldn't, and the payoff from those experiments can far exceed the inconvenience.

10:38 General Magic died of too many resources
General Magic was a late-80s, early-90s startup with almost unlimited talent, money and resources, and it judged the direction of technology for the following decades correctly — on paper, they invented the iPhone. But Epstein says more startups die of indigestion than of starvation: because they could do anything, they did everything, and projects kept ballooning out of control. They never clearly defined who the customer was (the so-called Joe Sixpack — nobody knew who that was), and ended up building things for each other rather than solving a specific problem. Internally, a low-level service engineer built a prototype of eBay and handed it to the company, and it was rejected as "too small, it'll never amount to anything." Epstein argues they should have started from smaller goals and smaller milestones.

12:41 A world without constraints is fiction
Tim Harford raises a disagreement: General Magic wasn't without constraints, it's just that all its constraints were long-term, so they could pretend the constraints didn't exist until money and time actually ran out. Epstein partly agrees, but corrects that they weren't short of money — they had more than they could spend — what they lacked was time. He cites Oliver Burkeman's view: believing that with the right productivity tools you can get everything done may just be a refusal to face your own mortality, a refusal to prioritize ruthlessly. About two-thirds of the former General Magic employees he interviewed said they simply couldn't figure out what not to do. Epstein treats this as a parable for the AI era: when the cost of starting something approaches zero, it removes the hard work of deciding what not to do, which may be one reason adoption has risen unprecedentedly while productivity hasn't risen correspondingly.

14:42 The Hemingway principle against urgency
Epstein calls his own writing method the Hemingway principle: Hemingway stopped mid-sentence, so the next day he knew which important place to return to. The last thing Epstein does at the end of each workday is designate which important place to start from the next day. He says this guards against the two main ways a workday goes off the rails: first, falling into an algorithmic feed or inbox first thing in the morning; second, the so-called mere urgency effect — people prioritize what feels urgent (like answering email) over what's truly important, even when the important thing objectively deserves more time.

17:44 Pre-registration made miracle drugs disappear
Before 2000, psychology was full of counterintuitive findings: thinking of Florida makes you walk more slowly, power poses raise testosterone, hurricanes with female names are more dangerous. Medicine was the same — almost every NIH-funded cardiovascular drug trial found a positive result; after 2000, new trials were almost all negative. The turning point was the NIH forcing researchers to constrain their behavior: write down your prediction in advance and stick to it. Epstein explains the mechanism: researchers would make a prediction, and when it didn't hold, they'd dig through a large dataset for a correlation, then retroactively invent a prediction, so that at publication it looked like they'd been looking for this from the start. Digging through data amounts to running nearly infinite tests, and each test raises the probability of a false positive, so a false-positive association is almost guaranteed.

20:45 Everything in the fridge both causes and prevents cancer
Epstein's favorite "dark humor paper" aggregated all nutrition research and found that almost every food you can think of has been shown in different studies to both cause and prevent cancer — with the exception of bacon, which was only found to cause it. He also tells the case of nutrition star researcher Brian Woznick: he did the famous bottomless soup bowl experiment, where people ate far more when an unseen tube kept refilling their soup. Later he wrote a blog post describing his research method: when a prediction didn't hold, he'd hand the data to a graduate student and say "find me something positive," and she never failed. Epstein's analogy: it's like firing randomly at a wall, then finding the densest cluster of bullet holes and painting a bullseye and a ten-ring around it — passersby marvel at the marksmanship. Most of Woznick's life's work was eventually retracted, and his research had been cited in a Nobel laureate's book.

27:51 Entrepreneurs who write predictions fail more but succeed more
Epstein extends pre-registration to personal life: when making a behavior change (say, wanting to exercise more), first write down what you plan to try and predict what it will bring, then do it, then check whether the prediction came true — this educates your intuition. He cites a randomized controlled study: entrepreneurs randomly assigned to a "scientific method training" group or an ordinary market research group; those trained falsified their own prior beliefs more often, discovering that the value they thought they were adding to the market didn't hold up, and as a result they pivoted more often and succeeded more often.

item.title: California Passed a Law Just to Shut Up a 24-Year-Old Blogger
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-加州为了让一个-24-岁博主闭嘴-专门立了一部法/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-加州为了让一个-24-岁博主闭嘴-专门立了一部法/
item.description: California's counterattack on an investigator isn't denial, it's legislation: the moment he uploads footage he's captured, he's fined $4,000 first, then pays the other side's legal fees. The person who introduced the law is the wife of the state attorney general.
item.content:encoded:
California's counterattack on an investigator isn't denial, it's legislation: the moment he uploads footage he's captured, he's fined $4,000 first, then pays the other side's legal fees. The person who introduced the law is the wife of the state attorney general.

The first half is the ledger of California high-speed rail; the second half is how a blogger with no journalism training used undercover filming to force arrests and legislation. High information density, but the stance is unmistakable.

0:08 $15 billion of high-speed rail leading to nowhere
The first number Nick Shirley's new film gives is $15 billion, 18 years, and the number of towns California high-speed rail connects so far is zero. When it was approved in 2008, it promised to connect Los Angeles and San Francisco; that same year China started building its own high-speed rail, and today it has connected more than 30,000 miles and covers the entire country, while California's segment connects nothing. He calls it the ‘high-speed rail to nowhere’—not a figure of speech: walk along the route and all you see is concrete and rebar. To finish it, another $100 to $200 billion is needed.

1:09 Cost went from $33 billion to $236 billion
The next part of the same ledger: the original estimate was $33 billion, jumped to $126 billion, and the latest estimate is $236 billion. By that number, it would become the third most expensive infrastructure project in world history—first is the 1950s interstate highway system, second is the International Space Station. Interviewees say the difference is: you can drive I-5 or I-80 across the country, you can go to space, but ‘we will never ride California high-speed rail.’ The name he gives this segment is ‘the most expensive piece of concrete known to man,’ while people in the Central Valley call it a modern Stonehenge. Newsom himself admitted in a privately recorded 2016 clip that he did not believe the project would be built in our lifetimes.

3:09 A third of the money goes to delay compensation
A third of the $15 billion goes to ‘change order delays’—because the builders don't know where the infrastructure is or how to build it. Contractors therefore got compensation rights: $170,000 per day, $5 million per month, simply because they couldn't start work. This February, California just settled a delay settlement of over $500 million, the largest delay settlement. Meanwhile, California still hasn't bought high-speed rail trains; Nick's judgment is that it's because they know there will never be a train on the tracks. Another calculation he makes: at current ridership, buying one-way tickets directly, $15 billion would subsidize free one-way tickets from San Francisco to Los Angeles for 150 years; at $236 billion, it would subsidize 300 years.

9:11 The state senator says it's happening
State Senator Cortezi just pushed through $1 billion a year for 20 consecutive years. Nick asked him face to face: not an inch of track has been laid in California, how do you explain that? He said ‘it's happening,’ and asked the reporter whether he had been there. Pressed that Newsom had privately said it was impossible, his answer was ‘maybe he did, maybe he didn't.’ Asked whether the high-speed rail authority had ever been held accountable for delays and overruns, he said ‘we're trying to hold them accountable.’ His justification wasn't transportation but that this is the largest economic development project in the country, and no other project in the country can compare. That same afternoon at 4:09 PM, Nick walked into the California High-Speed Rail Authority office—no one was there, even though they don't get off until 5.

12:11 California passed a law named after him
California passed AB2624, which legislators call the ‘Stop Nick Shirley Act’: as long as an ‘immigration service provider’—including nonprofits and medical institutions—sends him a demand letter, he cannot upload the video he filmed; uploading first incurs a $4,000 fine, then court, and if he loses he also has to pay the other side's legal fees. He says the law only appeared after his exposé, and he is suing California on the grounds that it is unconstitutional. Co-sponsor Chura took $80 million in government funding to do immigration advocacy; the person who introduced the bill is Mia Bont, wife of the state attorney general, whose job is precisely to prosecute fraud. On the very day this episode was recorded, the California DOJ charged 12 people in a $10 million fraud case, in the San Diego daycare he had filmed.

21:17 They hate him because he didn't pick a side
Jason's mechanism is: these people were idealistic once too, they wanted to bravely expose things, but they got captured, politicized, picked a side, so a person who doesn't pick a side is a threat to them. The way they criticize him isn't by saying he filmed it wrong, but that his fact-checking isn't rigorous enough. Jason's rebuttal is that none of that matters: what matters is he found real fraud, put people on camera, and then those people were charged, and he's the only one doing it. He says this used to be the job of 60 Minutes and Frontline, and they forgot how. Nick adds: no one in the mainstream media ever came to ask him how he did it, they all came to investigate him.

22:17 One video made the governor drop his re-election bid
The scale of the Minnesota daycare episode even he didn't expect: after the video was released, there were disturbances and protests locally; he says politicians encouraged people to take to the streets because with ICE present, the crowd could cover up the fraud. The result was Tim Walz dropping his re-election bid; the head of a money-laundering center who took $4 million tried to fly to London on a one-way ticket, was arrested for daycare fraud, and has already pleaded guilty; he says the same area also broke the largest autism fraud case in history at the same time. He attributes this output to rhythm rather than inspiration: for two and a half years he posted one video a week, and tipsters would proactively tell him where to go.

27:17 The next honeypot is welfare fraud
What he's going to dig into next is welfare fraud, which in his words is ‘absolutely insane’: in Portland, Oregon, a strip club can swipe SNAP cards; adult day care, hospice, anywhere that takes government money is full of fraud. The cost falls on personal safety: he now has to have security, because people really want to kill him. What he thinks about repeatedly before sleep is—will a fraudster, realizing they're finished, just shoot, so the video never gets out. The antidote proposed on the show is to have viewers pay for him to have researchers and security, on the grounds that Vice President J.D. Vance said 10% to 20% of tax revenue is wasted.

item.description: Legacy automakers didn't miss Tesla; they filed it as a new toy in a niche segment. What actually got disrupted was the seven-year model cycle, the dealer system and supply-chain interests — baggage that keeps them from turning around.
item.content:encoded:
Legacy automakers didn't miss Tesla; they filed it as a new toy in a niche segment. What actually got disrupted was the seven-year model cycle, the dealer system and supply-chain interests — baggage that keeps them from turning around.

An executive who spent over a decade at Mercedes, Aston Martin and Jaguar Land Rover explains that what foreign automakers missed wasn't technology, it was the rules. The second half on going global and management is especially valuable.

11:04 Tesla was filed as a new toy in a niche segment
Freda revisits how Mercedes judged it at the time: legacy automakers didn't miss Tesla, they categorized it as ‘a new product in a niche segment’, a functional replacement for one powertrain. When luxury customers said buying a Tesla was a status symbol, an innovation label, Mercedes' reaction was — you have five or six cars in your garage, adding one more is fine, you won't end up far from a traditional luxury brand. The error in that judgment was failing to see that EVs opened up a new business model and redefined the automobile product. She draws the Kodak analogy: when digital cameras arrived, Kodak also thought it might be a new toy for enthusiasts.

13:05 Direct sales is only the most superficial change
Freda says Tesla was the first brand to switch from dealer sales to direct sales, the most obvious change from the customer side, but behind it are bigger things: changes in suppliers and the supply chain, and changes in the speed of new-car development. These were only realized later. She stresses that legacy automakers realized Tesla was taking customers and having an effect on the market, but ‘still didn't fully realize whether EV would change the competitive rules of the auto industry’.

17:13 Turning a ship of hundreds of thousands is hard in process, not awareness
Freda says legacy automakers weren't unaware that digitalization was needed, but ‘an enterprise of hundreds of thousands, such a big ship turning around to make this change, the process is extremely, extremely difficult’. At the time sales were doubling every year and dealers could open 50 new stores a year; digitization was like a new initiative, a new campaign, done from headquarters to region, but resistance was strong and the process long. She gives the website example: many brands' websites are still centrally controlled by headquarters today, while Chinese consumers' online interaction habits are more sophisticated and they need more information — this communication process is extremely long.

21:19 Global consistency overrides Chinese consumer needs
Freda explains why headquarters is reluctant to delegate: branding has always been about global consistency. Luxury brands especially insist ‘you can't follow trends, trends may pass in the blink of an eye’, and must stick to brand tonality and a globally consistent look and feel. The website absolutely won't be delegated; only China-specific platforms like mini-programs can be used by the China team to persuade headquarters. But even then, headquarters needs to be convinced to let go — every time headquarters visits they ask why the materials headquarters gave you can't be used in China, why you need Xiaohongshu. She says such questions are ‘very dumb’, but the China team still has to persuade them every day.

28:30 A century-old rulebook disrupted by six-month iteration
Freda says the gasoline car industry has been in Germany for over a hundred years, many brands are over a hundred years old, and the rules of the game were set by these players over a century. Chinese, Korean and Japanese brands all entered playing by these rules: car updates were a seven-year generation major facelift, a five-year minor facelift, and it had been like that for decades. But today an EV might come out with a new feature every six months, and won't let your process run — ‘the entire rulebook of the auto industry has been completely disrupted’. Her personal judgment is that legacy automakers haven't realized how revolutionary the change is.

31:27 Supply chain and dealers are baggage they can't carry
Freda breaks down why legacy automakers can't turn around: German companies have Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers behind them, with decades of cooperation with the brand — you can't just cut off the engine supplier the moment you don't need engines; the dealer system has been in place for so many years, protecting dealer profitability is a rule everyone must follow, a brand can't say I don't care about five or six hundred dealers, I'll sell directly to consumers. Chinese EV newcomers start as EV from day one, can set their own rules, can be half dealers half direct sales, ‘without so much baggage’. Legacy automakers carry countless pieces of baggage, and it can't be changed overnight.

41:41 2023 Shanghai Auto Show: BYD put Yangwang next to Mercedes
Freda says the 2023 Shanghai Auto Show was the first after the pandemic; in the past foreign Global CEOs and global R&D presidents would come to China several times a year, but in those years visas were hard and quarantine was required, so visits dropped a lot, causing a huge surprise in 2023. She checked the data: there were about 100, 130, 150 new products in 2023, of which Chinese brands accounted for 100, 70% were pure electric. Which hall and what position at the auto show is very particular; luxury brands are all together, BBA each bring a luxury brand. But that year, for the first time, BYD put Yangwang next to Mercedes, in the same hall, and began the high-end positioning of domestic brands.

50:52 Betting on gasoline, hybrid and EV at once — where's the focus?
Freda says this is a huge strategic question she hasn't figured out: EV companies like NIO, Li Auto and Xpeng only have EVs and hybrids to invest in, but legacy automakers have gasoline cars, hybrids and EVs, and must also invest in R&D and new product production, with limited capital — where is the focus? Worse, China is in a state of EVs running forward, while Europe relaxed standards and the US and Canada completely withdrew EV sales subsidies; only China, such a large market, is running fast. She believes these foreign companies in China today ‘please no one, and do no product well’.

item.content:encoded:
Only one of the four guests had actually paid with an Agent, and it cost him just over 40 yuan. Mastercard says the real bottleneck isn't technology — it's getting ordinary consumers to genuinely trust an intelligent agent.

A live roundtable at the Bund Summit, with four guests representing payment networks, phone makers, models and platforms. Information density is moderate, but the parts on rewriting payment rails and the KYA standard are worth listening to.

4:25 Agent commerce is stuck in a chicken-and-egg problem
Han Xinyi said that since Q4 last year everyone has been very optimistic about Agentic Commerce, but actual implementation this year has been much slower than expected. From conversations with merchants, he sees a ‘chicken-or-egg’ deadlock: users want to use it, but merchants don't have good Agent services; merchants see no users using it, so they dare not invest in development. His solution is for Ant to act as a catalyst — using a metaphor from chemistry he learned as a child, potassium chlorate turning into oxygen needs manganese dioxide. The concrete action is the ‘Wishing Wall’ at the Alipay forum that afternoon, letting users write down what they want an Agent to do, then using incentive policies to push developers to build usable, useful Agents, to get the flywheel spinning first.

8:06 Payment networks were designed for humans in the loop
Jorn Lambert said that all systems today are designed for human participation — either the consumer themselves or the merchant — and now they must be redesigned. He broke it down into three problems to solve: first, identity authentication, confirming the instruction really comes from the person, not someone else using your account; second, confirming that the entity executing the task is a real, trusted agent, not a malicious bot; third, the consumer's instruction must be sufficiently clear — he said ‘tomorrow evening’ is not clear whether it means 6 p.m. or 9 p.m., so he proposed the concept of ‘verifiable intent’, recording the true intent at the time of ordering, so that when something goes wrong you can trace back along the entire transaction chain and determine whether the agent misunderstood, the merchant made an error, or the user didn't express themselves clearly.

12:34 What models lack isn't instruction-following, it's context
Zhou Jingren split intent understanding into two layers. Instruction-following ability has improved substantially over the past few years and is getting stronger today, but in practice models often feel insufficiently understanding of the individual, mainly due to lack of context — a person's understanding of something is a comprehensive judgment based on long-term discussion partners and historical conversation records, which today's models do not have, and an Agent System needs to effectively organize the relevant information. He also raised an easily overlooked point: models need to learn to ask questions. Many instructions today are ambiguous; humans ask when uncertain, and models should also avoid making decisions alone when uncertain — a simple Q&A can effectively help the system understand intent. At the task execution level, he emphasized sandboxes, permission management, traceability and auditability, and that these are not entirely up to the model — the model and the Agent Harness must jointly create the environment.

16:12 KYA is the new layer after KYC
Han Xinyi summarized trust and security into five layers: authorization, identity, Agent capability assessment, fund security and anti-fraud, and blockchain-based traceability and auditability. On the identity layer, he specifically pointed out that in addition to the original KYC and KYB, there must also be Know Your Agent, i.e., KYA. On the capability assessment layer, he said frankly that everyone is doing very little — why should I trust that a merchant's Agent can well meet my needs? The value of traceability is that when something goes wrong, the system can automatically determine who made the mistake: the user authorized incorrectly, their own Agent didn't understand clearly, information was transmitted incorrectly, or the merchant's Agent had an execution problem. Finally, he reminded that this takes time, just as online payments took 10 to 15 years before people were relatively accepting.

19:16 The real bottleneck isn't technology, it's consumers
Jorn Lambert compared this to building standards for e-commerce 25 years ago: back then, typing your card number into a merchant's website felt very nerve-wracking, but now no one worries, because over the years consumers have been shown that protections are provided, and there are recourse and remediation mechanisms when problems arise. He said we now need to prove it again, and are setting up standards one by one — identity, KYA, intent confirmation. Next, two things: getting thousands of companies worldwide to connect to this system, and getting consumers to believe the mechanism really works. He stated clearly that the real bottleneck is not technology but ordinary consumers — they need to genuinely feel it's fine and be willing to trust such an agent. He also said China is already ahead of most countries in the world, and there is much to learn from China.

22:55 The Pilates class test exposes a permissions problem
Hong Jun gave an example: asking the model to book a Monday Pilates class at the gym, the Agent found that time slot was fully booked for two weeks, so it wrote a program to delete all the previous users and squeeze you in. Zhou Jingren's response was that what matters more is which of your tasks today are authorized to the Agent — you ask it to book an appointment, can it simultaneously have the permission to delete others? He said just treat the Agent as a person; when giving a person instructions, you also give constraints. What the model side needs to do is distinguish which are hard constraints and which are just data seen while processing the task — it cannot, just because it read a document saying it must be over 200 yuan, drop the original constraint of under 100 yuan. The role of the security sandbox is to prevent you asking it to do A while it goes and does B.

26:20 Traffic will shift from time spent to intent
Han Xinyi laid out new opportunities that could grow on Ant's platform. First, traffic shifting from time spent to intent; the path of a personal assistant is becoming clearer, and he summarized several consensus features: personalized, somewhat proactive, full-modal interaction, long time series, and not just on phones — many startups are also doing it via applications. Second, merchant-side marketing conversion: if traffic shifts from time spent to intent, merchant marketing will shift from buying traffic to improve conversion rates to solving problems based on individual user intent, becoming more precise. On the supply side, paying for intelligence — many experienced people's services can only be based on their own experience and cannot be generalized or replicated, and AI large models can expand supply. He finally used a neuron analogy: there are over 7 billion people on Earth, assuming each has 10 Agents that's 70 billion; the human brain has 86 billion neurons, each with 3,000 connections. If the Agent economy reaches the same scale and connection depth, the generalization-driven business opportunities could be enormous.

31:15 Agents don't have bank cards; credentials must be rebuilt
Jorn Lambert said that today an agent doesn't have a bank card, nor a payment account like Alipay; it needs a completely different kind of credential, and that credential carries permissions. Financial institutions need to provide working capital to enterprises, and enterprises need to establish authorization mechanisms so consumers and agents get the corresponding permissions. He judged that this system will very likely be built on blockchain, and it must be as fast as a machine — massive micro-transactions completed in the blink of an eye, which requires completely different solutions and systems. Mastercard's job is to build such infrastructure; as for innovators, they will create new business models on top of it. He also agreed with Han Xinyi: it's hard to predict what the future will look like; rather than trying to predict the future, it's better to lay the tracks first.
